summary: What teachers and institutions actually complain about in OMR, and the defences

defences.angle: Turning the "voices" complaints into defences that live in our own files. I read PLAN.md section 4 and 11, COMPETITIVE-NOTES section 5, paper.ts and spec.ts, and I checked every complaint against the pipeline as literally written rather than as intended. Four things fell out that are not opinions but defects I can point at in the repo, and they are the backbone of this list. (1) The documented rule "fill_i / max(fill), answer if > 0.65 and no second > 0.45" has no absolute floor, so a blank question with a single speck of dirt produces a CONFIDENT WRONG answer, and a genuinely clean blank question produces "ambiguous" and stops the teacher on every skipped question. Neither is "blank", and the DB already has the right representation for blank ('?' in scans.answers). (2) The pipeline decodes the QR after "resize x0.25". At codeModuleMm 0.5 and a 1080px-wide frame over 210mm that is 0.64 pixels per module, which is undecodable, so "it will not scan" is built into the current pipeline. (3) BubbleMetricsSchema permits overlapping bubbles: pitchXMm minimum 5, radiusMm maximum 3.5, so 2r = 7mm > 5mm pitch. pitchYMm min 6 and gridPitchYMm min 5 overlap the same way. There is no cross-field refinement. That is exactly the Scantron density complaint, schema-legal today. (4) Rule 3, "three consecutive frames agree", is not evidence when the phone is still and the lamp is fixed: a specular highlight sitting inside a filled bubble is stable across frames, so three frames agree on the same wrong answer. Agreement has to come from independent views, not from repetition. Beyond the repo, the highest-impact item in the whole set is regulatory, not technical, and I treat it that way. Note on sourcing: URLs below come from the researcher's cited findings; I could not independently re-fetch alyaum.com or sabq.org (egress-blocked) so the Saudi scope claim is relayed, not verified by me. All pixel and millimetre arithmetic is mine, derived from the constants in paper.ts and spec.ts, and is reasoning rather than citation.
defences.alreadyCovered: Do not re-bank these. Fully answered already: fractional question weights (points real[] answers competitor finding 44 exactly); alternate accepted answers discovered after the papers are marked (alternates jsonb plus answers-as-string means the whole class rescores with zero rescanning, which is a better answer than any competitor has); silent duplicate records from a rescan (rule 8 plus acceptance criterion 9, and criterion 9 is already written as an automated test); "ID: 0" invented from a blank grid (rule 9); paywall friction and locked buttons (section 12-1, zero gated features, which answers half of the Exam Reader "I paid and it still misreads" anger before it starts); multi-device licensing; the machine cannot read handwriting (the name crop capability is genuinely already specified, usage:'studentName' plus WrittenBoxLayout.box, and needs no spec work); a device that has never seen the template can still grade the paper (code:'full' carries the whole geometry, which quietly kills a large family of "wrong form" failures that competitors cannot avoid); the teacher never leaves scan mode (loop step 2); corner-lock feedback, which answers the geometry half of "it will not scan" (item 42); "I wish I could fit two sheets on one page", which PAPER_FAMILIES answers correctly by designing A5 and A6 at true size instead of scaling; offline operation, which is table stakes not a differentiator (competitor note 56 says so plainly). Partially answered, and the gap matters: acceptance criterion 8 covers shot-to-shot determinism on one paper on one day, but teachers are complaining about month-to-month variance, which a golden set of three shots per paper does not measure; rule 9 fixes the representation of a missing student id but not the workflow of resolving it; the relative-within-question threshold (rule 1) defeats shadow, which is a uniform darkening, but does nothing against a specular highlight, which is a localised brightening inside the one bubble the measurement depends on; discrimination factor is already noted (competitive finding 35) but only as an analysis feature, not as a live guard.
defences.cannotDefend: Five things no software fixes, and what we do anyway. First, a genuinely ambiguous mark. If a bubble sits at 50 percent fill there is no algorithm that knows what the student meant, and any product claiming otherwise is guessing. Our answer is to make refusal cheap and legible rather than rare: refusal costs nothing on the quota, names its own cause, and takes one tap to resolve. The self-critical consequence is that accuracy alone is a dishonest metric, including for us. We must publish the pair, accuracy on accepted papers AND refusal rate, because a 99.7 percent that hides a 15 percent refusal rate is the same lie as a competitor silently guessing. Section 8b commits us to publishing methodology, so publish both numbers or the methodology is decoration. Second, uniform print scaling is undetectable from the printed content alone. Everything on the sheet scales together, so no internal ratio reveals it. Only the paper edge (which a phone may not find against a cluttered desk) or a known page box (which the PDF path has exactly) exposes it. We therefore detect the consequences rather than the cause on the camera path, and detect the cause exactly on the PDF path, and we accept that a photocopied stack may simply be refused with "this sheet is not the geometry it claims". Third, a mistyped answer key. No scan can know the truth. The discrimination warning is a statistical hint that needs roughly ten papers before it is trustworthy, so the first papers of every batch are structurally unprotected, and we should say that rather than imply the guard is always on. Fourth, a Ministry prohibition is not an engineering problem. If the ban on phone applications for grading covers what we sell, no accuracy number overrides it. The only real defences are scope (sell into formative classroom quizzes, not final exams, and say so in the plan before launch rather than discovering it after), the directorate approval process (which exists and has named conditions, so treat it as a product surface with real artifacts), and the fact that our strongest privacy decision happens to be the exact compliance argument for the rule against photographing student answers. Fifth, handwriting. We do not read it, deliberately, and once we stop storing images the name crop dies when the card closes. A dispute over whose paper this is will always need the physical sheet. Say that out loud in the product rather than let a teacher discover it during an argument with a parent.

requirements.complaint: "Bright Light Detected": glare on the pencil marks makes the sheet unreadable or, worse, read wrong. ZipGrade's own help centre says this has historically caused more mismarks than any other issue.
requirements.defence: Graphite is specular, so the brightest pixel on the page can sit inside a filled bubble and every darkness measure inverts on exactly the bubble the answer depends on. Rule 1 does not save us because normalising by max(fill) normalises against a corrupted maximum. Three defences. (a) Measure two statistics per bubble, not one: darkness AND variance inside the disc. At the warp to 1000x1414 a 4mm bubble is about 19px across, so the disc holds roughly 283 pixels, ample for both. A blank bubble is uniform paper (low darkness, low variance). A filled bubble is uniform graphite (high darkness, low variance). A glared filled bubble is high variance with mid darkness, and that signature is unmistakable. (b) Saturation gate: count pixels at or above 250/255 in the disc. If more than about 15 percent of the disc is blown out, the bubble is not light, it is unmeasurable, and it goes to uncertain, never to empty. (c) Direction, not scolding: compute which quadrant of the warped page carries the saturated cluster and say in Arabic which way to move the phone, because the teacher cannot act on "bad lighting".
requirements.where: scanner pipeline for the two statistics and the saturation gate, interface for the directional instruction
requirements.testable: A named glare stratum in the golden set: the same papers shot under a direct point light positioned to put the highlight inside filled bubbles. The pass condition is not accuracy, it is zero silent wrong answers. Allowed outcomes are correct read or refusal, and a wrong answer on a glare paper fails the build outright.

requirements.complaint: Lightly or partially shaded bubbles are skipped and the student is scored zero for an answer they gave, and conversely blank questions get confidently answered.
requirements.defence: The documented rule is fill_i/max(fill), answer if > 0.65 and no second > 0.45. Trace it on a blank question. If the row is genuinely clean, all fills are near-equal noise, the second-highest ratio lands above 0.45, and the question is reported ambiguous, so a student who skipped five questions stops the teacher five times. If the row has one speck of dirt or a printed artifact at roughly three times the others, the ratio is 1.0 with the second at 0.33, and we emit a CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER. Neither outcome is "blank", and scans.answers already has the right symbol for blank ('?'). Fix: gate the ratio behind an absolute floor. max(fill) must clear minInkRatio (start at 0.15 of the disc) before any ratio is computed; below it the question is BLANK, full stop. Make the floor safe under shadow by defining darkness against a local paper reference: sample paper white from an annulus just outside each bubble, excluding the printed outline ring, so "dark" is per-bubble relative to its own neighbourhood. That keeps rule 1's shadow immunity while giving us the floor it lacks. Two more clauses: if every bubble in a question clears the floor, that is ambiguous, not "the max wins"; and compute the fill on the warped GREYSCALE, never on the binary image produced for fiducial detection, because binarising throws away the exact gradation the fill ratio exists to preserve.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline
requirements.testable: Pure TypeScript unit tests in core-omr on synthetic images, no camera needed, which is exactly the plan section 13 order. Assert: a clean blank row returns '?' 100 percent of the time; a blank row with a single injected speck at 3x, 5x and 10x the noise floor returns '?' and never a letter; a faint but real single mark above the floor returns that letter; a select:'many' question is split by floor plus gap, never by ratio-to-max, which is meaningless when several bubbles are legitimately filled.

requirements.complaint: "Some days it works smoothly, other days it will not scan anything." Non-determinism experienced as unreliability, which destroys trust rather than merely costing time.
requirements.defence: Rule 3 as written is repetition, not evidence. A phone held still under a fixed lamp gives three identical frames, so three frames agree on the same wrong answer and we have proved nothing. Three changes. (a) Require pose diversity: the three accepted frames must differ, with the projected page corners moving at least about 2 percent of page width (roughly 20px at the 1000px warp) or the estimated view angle changing by 3 degrees or more between them. Agreement across genuinely different views is evidence. (b) When the pose is static past about 1.5 seconds, which is the tripod and document-scanner case, fall back to a deterministic perturbation ensemble: re-sample the bubbles k times under fixed perturbations (plus and minus 1.5 degrees rotation, plus and minus 2 percent scale, 1px grid translation) and require identical answers across all k. Cost is only the sampling stage, about 200 bubbles times 283 pixels times 4 passes, roughly 226 thousand pixel reads, negligible against the 400ms budget in criterion 2. This same ensemble is how we prove criterion 8 in CI with no phone at all, and it is the substitute for frame agreement on the future PDF path where consecutive frames do not exist. (c) Stratify the golden set by environment, not just by count: classroom fluorescent, window backlight, evening tungsten, phone flash, photographer's own shadow, across at least three phone models. CI must report accuracy PER STRATUM, because an aggregate 99.7 percent can conceal a stratum at 92 percent that is somebody's every Tuesday, which is precisely what "some days" means.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline for pose diversity and the ensemble, process for golden set composition and CI reporting
requirements.testable: CI fails if any single environment stratum falls below a named floor (98 percent) even when the aggregate passes. Separately, the perturbation ensemble runs across the entire golden set and the build fails if any one paper yields two different accepted scores, which turns criterion 8 from a three-shot sample into an exhaustive check.

requirements.complaint: "It will not scan" with no useful explanation. The single highest-traffic support topic in the category.
requirements.defence: The pipeline as documented cannot decode our own code. It reads: resize x0.25, then later, decode QR. With codeModuleMm 0.5 and a 1080px-wide frame across 210mm we have 5.14 px/mm, so a module is 2.57px at full resolution and 0.64px after the 0.25 downscale. That is undecodable, so "will not scan" is currently designed in. Fix: use the downscaled frame ONLY for fiducial detection, then take the homography from that cheap pass, project the code's known rectangle back into the FULL resolution frame, and decode from that crop. Enforce a measured minimum of 3 pixels per module on the crop, which at 0.5mm modules means the page must span at least about 1260px in the capture. If the frame does not meet it, refuse with "come closer" rather than failing silently. This costs nothing: the crop is a few hundred pixels square, not the whole frame.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline
requirements.testable: Unit test in core-omr over rendered sheets at descending capture widths (1920, 1440, 1280, 1080, 720 across the page). Assert the decoder succeeds down to the stated pixels-per-module floor and returns the named "move closer" refusal below it, never a generic failure. Then assert the full-frame crop path decodes on frames where the x0.25 path provably cannot.

requirements.complaint: Sheets were photocopied, or printed with Fit to page, or A4 on Letter, and now nothing scans. Institutions publish this as standing instruction, not as troubleshooting.
requirements.defence: Our printed warning puts the burden on someone reading fine print at the moment of least attention, and it is printed in the one place the failure destroys. Give the timing bar a second job instead. Fit the homography from the four corners, then project every expected timing-mark centre and measure the reprojection residual against the detected marks. At the 1000px per 210mm warp one pixel is 0.21mm, so a residual gate at 0.5mm RMS is about 2.4px, comfortably measurable. Corners forced to match plus interior disagreement is the universal signature of a geometry that is not the geometry the code claims: anisotropic scaling, photocopier stretch, curl, wrong template. Gate the frame on it and name the reason. Match the timing marks with outlier rejection (trimmed median residual or RANSAC) so a stray pen line that occludes or adds a few marks cannot shift row indexing, which is the exact failure institutional scoring centres warn about. State explicitly that neither feature alone is mandatory: we need four corners, OR three corners plus at least four timing marks solved by least squares under the same residual gate, which is also the degraded path for a bent corner. On the PDF path the page box is known exactly, so the fiducial position inside it is a direct scale measurement, and marginMm is 6 so a 96 percent print on A4 pushes the margin to about 9.96mm, a 66 percent increase, roughly 19px, trivially detectable.
requirements.where: sheet design (the timing bar stops being decoration and becomes an instrument), scanner pipeline
requirements.testable: Print one template at 100, 98, 96 and 94 percent and as A4-fit-to-Letter, then scan all five. Assert no scaled sheet is ever graded silently, and that the refusal names geometry as the cause. Synthetic occlusion test in core-omr: black out k of N timing marks and inject k spurious ones, assert row indexing is unchanged for k up to 20 percent. Three-corner recovery is proven by the criterion 8 rule extended to damage: a paper with one corner physically folded must produce the same result as the intact scan of the same paper.

requirements.complaint: The dominant named cause of scan failure is bookkeeping, not optics: "the application is expecting a different answer sheet than the physical form being scanned." The teacher printed form X and selected quiz Y.
requirements.defence: We are more exposed here than ZipGrade, not less, because we actively encourage template reuse (templates and exams are separate tables, competitive finding 31). The QR carries templateId, so we catch the wrong TEMPLATE. We cannot catch the far more common error: right template, wrong EXAM, because two exams sharing the 50-question template print byte-identical sheets, and class B's papers land in class A's exam with no signal at all. That is data corruption, not a scan failure. Fix: two print modes. A bound sheet carries examId in the code alongside templateId and formCode, and is the default when printing from inside an exam, costing nothing at print time. A generic sheet carries the template alone and stays available for leftover stacks, and the teacher owns that trade the same way they own code:'short'. Detection is not the deliverable: a bound sheet scanned into the wrong exam must name the exam it actually belongs to and offer a one-tap switch, because a refusal that does not say which quiz this is leaves the teacher exactly where the competitor leaves them.
requirements.where: sheet design (code payload), interface (named refusal and the switch), process (default to bound when printing from an exam)
requirements.testable: Automated: open exam B, scan a sheet bound to exam A. Assert zero rows written to B, assert the refusal names A, assert the one-tap switch moves the session to A and grades the paper there. Then scan a generic sheet into both exams and assert both succeed, so the escape hatch is not accidentally closed.

requirements.complaint: Customer service cannot help, because the cause is physical: their printer, their lamp, their students' pencils. Teachers stop using a product they cannot get an answer about.
requirements.defence: The mitigation is not a bigger support team, it is an app that diagnoses the physical cause and says so in words the teacher can act on. Every refusal must carry a cause from a CLOSED enumeration and a physical instruction, never a generic failure. The enumeration falls straight out of the pipeline stages: corners not found (which corners, highlighted, already item 42); light reflecting off the page (which quadrant, which way to move); page not flat or not this geometry (timing-mark residual, from the geometry requirement); code unreadable (come closer, with the distance implied by the pixels-per-module floor); sheet belongs to another exam (named); sheet printed at the wrong scale. A refusal without a cause code should be impossible to construct in the type system, so the enum is the return type, not a string. Second half: keep a local, image-free tally of refusal causes so the teacher can see "12 refusals this week, 10 of them glare", which turns "it is touchy" into "your lamp is behind you" without a single byte leaving the device.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline (cause is part of the result type), interface (the instruction and the weekly tally)
requirements.testable: Exhaustiveness test: every refusal path in core-omr returns a member of the enum, enforced by a TypeScript never-check so a new failure mode cannot compile without a message. Then a golden-set audit asserting the cause emitted matches the injected defect for each stratum (glare papers report glare, folded papers report geometry, and so on) at above 90 percent, because a confidently wrong diagnosis is worse than none.

requirements.complaint: The student ID grid is blank, wrong, or does not match the roster, so the teacher fixes it by hand. Every product in the category has built the same reconciliation screen, which is the strongest possible evidence that it happens on a meaningful fraction of every batch. The same hazard exists for the version or set code, where an unfilled code makes the whole sheet score zero.
requirements.defence: Rule 9 fixed the representation. The workflow is still missing, and the material for it is already in the product and merely unconnected. On the confirmation card, when the id reads unset or reads an id absent from the roster, show the name crop beside a shortlist that is not arbitrary: the students in the selected class who have NO paper yet in this exam. Mid-batch in a 30-student class that list is typically five to ten names, so this is a one-tap pick, not a search. Second, extend rule 9 verbatim to the key version field, which is the same machinery already (BubbleGridFieldSchema with usage:'keyVersion'), with one policy clause: if the exam has exactly one active key, an unset version resolves to it silently because there is nothing to be ambiguous about; if the exam has two or more keys, an unset version HOLDS the paper and asks. Never default to key A when more than one key exists, which is the OMR-vendor failure where a blank set code scores the whole sheet zero.
requirements.where: interface (the card and the shortlist), scanner pipeline (unset as an explicit state on both grids)
requirements.testable: Seeded end-to-end test: 30-student roster, 30 papers of which 6 have blank ids, assert every paper is matched in at most one tap and zero mismatches. Separately: exam with 2 keys and a paper with a blank version bubble must be HELD, asserted by the absence of a graded row; the same paper in a 1-key exam must grade with no prompt.

requirements.complaint: The bubbles are too small and too tightly spaced, so students overshoot the edges and mis-bubble whole lines. The most common student-side complaint about bubble sheets.
requirements.defence: This is a live defect in spec.ts, not a hypothetical. BubbleMetricsSchema allows radiusMm up to 3.5 and pitchXMm down to 5, so 2r = 7mm against a 5mm pitch: OVERLAPPING BUBBLES ARE SCHEMA-LEGAL TODAY. pitchYMm minimum 6 and gridPitchYMm minimum 5 overlap the same way against the same maximum radius. The bounds are per-field with no cross-field refinement, so nothing in the type system prevents a generator from emitting exactly the Scantron density students are complaining about. Fix: add a z.refine enforcing pitch >= 2 * radius + minBubbleGapMm on all three pitches, with the gap floor derived from the scan side rather than from taste. The default geometry gives 5.6 minus 4 = 1.6mm of edge-to-edge gap, about 7px at the warp, so set the floor at 1.5mm and refuse anything tighter. Refusing is the right verb: this is the same protective pattern as codeMaxSizeMm, which already refuses a sheet rather than shrinking the code past readability. maxRowPitchMm and the PAPER_FAMILIES ladder already guard the sparse side well; this is the missing guard on the dense side.
requirements.where: sheet design (sheet-spec validation)
requirements.testable: Property test over the whole accepted spec space: for every combination of questions, choices, columns, paper and bubble metrics that the schema admits, assert edge-to-edge gap >= minBubbleGapMm on all three axes. The test should fail today against the current schema, which is the proof the defect is real, and pass after the refinement. Then assert the generator throws a named error for a 200-question dense spec rather than emitting a cramped sheet.

requirements.complaint: "I paid for the subscription and it still misreads, and every failed scan I retry burns another one of my allowance." Exam Reader, the closest thing to a direct Arabic-first incumbent, sits near 2.36 out of 5 across roughly 310 Google Play ratings, with reviewers reporting five or more attempts and each one consuming their quota.
requirements.defence: Metering the wrong event monetises our own defects and makes the free tier feel rigged instead of generous. usage.papers_graded is the right noun, but the plan never says what increments it. State it as a rule: papers_graded increments exactly once per distinct accepted paper. A refused frame, an ambiguous scan the teacher discards, a paper the teacher deletes, and a rescan reconciled onto an existing paper via rule 8 "replace" all increment NOTHING. "Keep both" does increment, because that is a deliberate teacher action creating a second paper. Second, make the promise visible: the quota in the navigation footer (design rule 15, competitive finding 51) must be watched NOT ticking during a rescan, because the number visibly not moving is the trust mechanism, not the accounting. Third, deletes must be handled by the sync design: derive each device's contribution as the count of distinct non-deleted papers it graded and sum across devices, rather than syncing a monotonic counter that a delete cannot walk back. That keeps the section 12-2 property (two devices never lose each other's count) while making a deletion actually refund. At 100 papers per month free, against a 26 riyal per year anchor, this is the whole difference between the tier reading as a gift and reading as a trap.
requirements.where: process and billing rules, database (usage derivation)
requirements.testable: Automated: scan the same paper five times choosing replace each time, assert papers_graded == 1 and scans row count == 1 (which also extends acceptance criterion 9). Scan then delete, assert 0. Emit ten refused frames, assert 0. Scan and choose keep both, assert 2. Run the same suite across two devices syncing into one org and assert the org total is 1, not 2.

requirements.complaint: "It crashed in the middle of a quiz and lost the grades, so I had to rescan every form." Less frequent than accuracy complaints, far more severe per occurrence.
requirements.defence: Batch-scoped state is the cause: if results live in memory until the session closes, a crash costs the whole stack. Our SQLite-first design structurally prevents it, but ONLY if the write happens per paper inside the scan loop, and the plan never states that ordering, which is exactly the kind of thing that gets optimised away later for frame-loop performance. Write the rule down: the SQLite insert commits in the same operation that produces the accepted result, BEFORE the confirmation card renders, and the card's delete action deletes a committed row rather than cancelling an uncommitted one. scans.id is UUIDv7 generated on device, so the write is naturally idempotent under retry and needs no coordination. The cost is one small transaction per paper, against a 400ms budget that is dominated by vision work, so there is no performance argument for batching it.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline and app boundary, database
requirements.testable: Kill test in CI: SIGKILL the app between paper 17 and 18 of a scripted 30-paper batch, restart, assert 17 rows present with correct scores and no partial or duplicated row. Run it against the real storage layer, at minimum as an integration test, and run it on every release, because this regresses silently.

requirements.complaint: The Saudi Ministry of Education has banned phone applications for grading exams, citing weak accuracy, and separately prohibits photographing students' answers by any means. Relayed from the researcher's Saudi press citations; I could not re-fetch those sources (egress-blocked) so treat the exact scope as needing one verification pass before it drives a launch decision.
requirements.defence: Our "images are never uploaded or stored" decision is not a privacy nicety here, it is the compliance argument for the literal prohibition on photographing student answers, and it is only worth anything if it is PROVABLE rather than promised. Harden it into an invariant with teeth: no camera frame, no warped image, and no name crop is ever written to disk, ever. The name crop lives in memory for the life of the confirmation card and is zeroed when the card closes. No image bytes cross the network, in any code path, including diagnostics and crash reporting, which is the usual leak. Then make the proof a thirty-second demonstration a directorate officer can run themselves: put the device in airplane mode and grade a paper. It works, therefore nothing left the device. That demo is acceptance criterion 3 repurposed as a compliance artifact, which costs us nothing we were not already building.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline invariant, process (the scripted demonstration)
requirements.testable: Filesystem and network audit during a 30-paper scan session: assert zero writes of image data to any path including caches and temp directories, and zero bytes to any host. Make it a CI gate, not a manual check. Add a crash-reporter test asserting no frame buffer can reach a report payload.

requirements.complaint: "It grades fine but I still have to type the scores into my gradebook by hand." The most-repeated FEATURE complaint in ZipGrade reviews, distinct from accuracy complaints, and described by reviewers as their only complaint.
requirements.defence: The product's value ends one step before the teacher's job does. Excel and CSV export is already in MVP scope, so the work is fidelity, not features, and the fidelity details are precisely what break Arabic school data. Four rules. (a) Export the student's external id exactly as it arrived from the imported roster CSV, byte for byte, unmodified, so a VLOOKUP against any school system always joins. (b) Write ids as TEXT, never numeric, so Excel cannot eat leading zeros, which is the classic destroyer of Saudi-style identifier keys. (c) UTF-8 with BOM on CSV, because Excel renders Arabic names as mojibake without it and the teacher concludes our export is broken. (d) Ship the column set as named presets rather than one fixed shape. The presets themselves are the after-MVP half and must be derived from REAL FILES: during the 20-teacher closed beta in weeks 13 to 14, collect the actual grade-entry file each teacher uses today and build the preset from that, not from documentation. The plan currently treats the Noor-compatible format as a known quantity; it is an unresearched assumption and should be labelled as one until a real file exists.
requirements.where: web dashboard export, process (beta collection of real files)
requirements.testable: Round-trip test: import a roster CSV with ids carrying leading zeros and Arabic names with tashkeel, grade, export, reopen in Excel, assert ids are byte-identical and Arabic renders correctly. Assert the same for the xlsx path. For the preset half, the acceptance is procedural and honest: no preset ships until it has been proven against a file a real teacher actually uploads.

requirements.complaint: A poorly erased answer is read as a second mark, so a correct answer is scored wrong. The most-repeated accuracy complaint in ZipGrade reviews, and exactly what we watched happen in competitor finding 49 where the same paper scored 4/9.5 and then 3/9.5 two minutes later.
requirements.defence: Routing erasures to ambiguous is correct and we already do it, but it means the ambiguity queue will be dominated by erasures rather than by genuine double-marks. Eraser residue sits at 20 to 45 percent fill, which is not noise, it is a systematically produced intermediate value present on a large share of real papers. If every erased answer stops the teacher, our scan loop stalls and we feel slower than the competitor that silently guesses, which is how a correct decision loses. The unexploited signal is spatial, not quantitative. Compute two more cheap statistics per bubble, on the pixels we are already touching: SPILL, the darkness in the annulus between r and 1.6r with the printed outline ring masked out, and COVERAGE UNIFORMITY, the fraction of disc pixels that are dark against the mean darkness. A deliberate mark is bounded and solid: high coverage, low spill, low variance, stopping at the printed outline. An erasure is diffuse and rubbed: moderate coverage, HIGH SPILL because the student rubbed across the paper, high variance. Rule: when exactly one bubble is a clean solid fill and the other candidate carries a positive erasure signature, resolve to the clean one and record a distinct resolved-erasure flag. This is a deliberate loosening of rule 2 and must be treated as one: we only auto-resolve on POSITIVE evidence of erasure, never on mere weakness, and it ships behind a measured false-resolve rate. Precondition: the spill and variance statistics ship in MVP alongside the glare work so tuning data exists before we write the policy.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, database (a distinct flag in scans.flags)
requirements.testable: A dedicated golden-set subset of at least 40 papers with deliberate erasures at varying vigour, hand-labelled. Two metrics, both required: zero auto-resolves that disagree with the human label (a single one blocks the feature), and a measured drop in the fraction of questions entering the ambiguity queue. Publish both numbers, because the second is the benefit and the first is the licence.

requirements.complaint: Teachers double-check scans by hand, which erodes the time saving the product is sold on. Telling detail: this appears in POSITIVE reviews, so even satisfied users do not trust unverified output.
requirements.defence: The cause is unquantified confidence. Because competitors return a boolean per bubble, the teacher cannot tell WHICH papers deserve checking, so cautious teachers check all of them and the five-minute grading claim becomes twenty. Our fill-ratio decision is the exact fix and its value is larger than the plan claims. Store one number per scan: minConfidence, the smallest decision margin across the paper, where margin is the gap between the top and second fill ratio on select:'one' questions, normalised. That is one real column beside the existing flags smallint. Then, at the end of a class stack, sort ascending and tell the teacher the thing they actually want to hear: "three of these thirty need your eyes, the other twenty-seven do not". Calibrate the threshold from measurement, not taste: set it on the golden set so every paper above it agreed with the human label, and publish the threshold and its derivation, which is precisely the documented-statistics play section 8b commits us to. The plan today surfaces per-scan counts (doubles, blanks, uncertain) but never aggregates them into the batch-level judgement the teacher needs at the end of the pile. MVP ships the column and a single end-of-batch line; the sorted review workflow is the after-MVP half.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline (emit the statistic), database (one column), interface (the batch triage)
requirements.testable: On the golden set, verify triage RECALL is 100 percent: every paper where the machine result differs from the human label must fall inside the flagged set. Then report PRECISION as the honest cost, meaning what fraction of flagged papers were actually fine. Publishing both is the difference between a claim and a measurement, and the recall number is the one that must never regress.

requirements.complaint: When a grade is challenged the teacher needs to show the paper, and institutional OMR workflows depend on a stored image of the form to resolve disputes without hunting for the physical sheet. Remark stores an image of every form for exactly this.
requirements.defence: This collides head-on with our strongest privacy decision AND with the Saudi rule against photographing student answers, so the resolution has to be better than a compromise. It is. Store the per-bubble fill ratios instead of an image: one byte per bubble, quantised 0 to 255. A 50-question 4-choice sheet plus a 6-digit id grid is 200 plus 60 bubbles, about 260 bytes; at 100 papers per month that is 26KB a month and roughly 312KB a year, against something like 20MB a month for JPEGs. Around 800 times smaller, and it contains no handwriting, no name, no face, so it is not personal data in the way a photograph is. The review screen then RE-RENDERS synthetically: the printed geometry is known exactly from the spec, which is the entire architecture, so we draw the sheet with each bubble shaded to its measured ratio and overlay the green and red rings from competitive finding 45. This is strictly better evidence than a photograph for our purpose, because it shows what the machine actually decided on rather than a picture a human re-interprets. Immediate MVP consequence, even before we build this: state in the plan that the section 4 review screen is LIVE-ONLY, so nobody builds a navigation path to a screen that cannot exist from stored data. Honest limit: it can never show handwriting, so a dispute about whose paper this is still needs the physical sheet.
requirements.where: database, interface, scanner pipeline (emit the blob)
requirements.testable: Recompute the answers from the stored ratio blob alone and assert byte-identical equality with scans.answers for every paper in the golden set, which proves the blob is a faithful record of the decision. Assert the blob stays under 400 bytes for a 100-question sheet. Assert the synthetic re-render is pixel-stable across runs so two teachers looking at the same dispute see the same picture.

requirements.complaint: The stated ground for the Saudi ban on phone grading applications is weak accuracy, and any school wanting to use automated grading must apply to its education directorate under named conditions with a committee empowered to suspend use. Relayed from the researcher's citations, not independently verified by me.
requirements.defence: Treat the approval process as a product surface with real artifacts, because that is what it is. Three deliverables. (a) A scope decision written into the plan BEFORE launch rather than discovered after: state whether we sell into formative classroom quizzes and short tests, which is ZipGrade's actual market and ours, or into final exams, which is where the prohibition bites hardest. One sentence, free, and it changes what we may say in marketing. (b) An Arabic approval pack aimed at the directorate officer signing the form, not at the teacher: the measured golden-set accuracy WITH its methodology, the refusal rate beside it, the determinism criterion, and the airplane-mode demonstration script. Our real numbers are already our GEO strategy under section 8b, so this is the same asset pointed at a second audience. (c) State the no-images policy in Arabic, in ministry vocabulary, on the marketing site and inside the app, since it answers the photography rule directly. Written in the ministry's own words it is a compliance argument; written in ours it is a privacy blurb nobody reads.
requirements.where: process, interface (the Arabic statement in-app), marketing site
requirements.testable: Not a unit test, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The proof is procedural: one real directorate application submitted during the closed beta, and the pack is judged by whether it survives that review without us being asked for anything we cannot supply. Also verifiable now and cheaply: re-fetch the Saudi sources from an unblocked network and confirm the exact scope of the ban before the scope sentence is written, because everything above depends on where that line actually falls.

requirements.complaint: The wrong answer key was applied, or a key was typed wrong, and a whole class's scores are wrong, silently, with every individual score looking plausible. University scoring services enumerate this as a standard checklist item.
requirements.defence: Our design already avoids the worst version, because the key is typed in the app rather than bubbled on paper and the form code selects among keys. But it introduces the mirror hazard: a teacher who mistypes one character gets a class of consistently wrong scores and no signal at all. A per-paper error costs one student; a key error costs a class. The detector is already in our notes as a nice-to-have (competitive finding 35) and is cheap: after N papers of the same exam and form, compute per question the proportion correct and the point-biserial discrimination. Flag a question when proportion correct falls below chance (25 percent on a 4-choice question) AND discrimination is negative. That conjunction is near-proof the key is wrong for that question rather than the question being hard, because a hard question is answered by the strong students and this one is not. Promote it from a later report to a warning shown DURING the scan session: "question 7, 2 of 12 correct, and the strongest students got it wrong, check the key". One tap to fix, and because answers are stored as strings every existing paper rescores instantly with no rescanning, which is the section 5 storage decision paying off a second time. Honest limit: it needs roughly 10 papers to be trustworthy, so N=5 shows a soft hint and N=10 a firm one.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline and analytics, interface (the in-session warning)
requirements.testable: Synthetic: take a golden exam with known-correct results, corrupt exactly one character of the key, run 20 papers through, assert the warning fires on that question and on no other. Run the uncorrupted key across every golden exam and assert ZERO false positives, because a warning that cries wolf on genuinely hard questions will be dismissed and then ignored when it matters.

requirements.complaint: Institutions are shutting Scantron down (Kentucky ending Spring 2026, UC Irvine ended July 2024, Iowa replaced for fall 2024, Penn State closed scanning operations), with one high school reporting over $5,000 a year on forms and machines around $3,000 plus $500 a year maintenance.
requirements.defence: The market is actively looking for an exit and our PDF-scan path lands into it, but note carefully what those institutions actually migrated TO: Gradescope, Canvas, LMS-integrated tools. Not other camera apps. The institutional buyer's requirement is LMS and SIS integration plus audit trail, not phone convenience, and that is a DIFFERENT PRODUCT from the MVP. The defence here is mostly refusing a mistake: do not assume the teacher app wins that buyer, and do not let institutional feature requests bend the teacher product. Two things to carry forward cheaply now, both already half-built. The org_id column in every table from day one is exactly right and costs nothing. The append-only audit log for grade changes in section 7 is the seed of the audit requirement that buyer will ask for, so keep it and make sure it records who changed what and when, not just that something changed. Also worth naming as a differentiator when we do sell there: Akindi documents grades landing in the WRONG COURSE when teachers submit from a departmental copier, and our exam-bound code solves that for free.
requirements.where: process and positioning, database (audit log shape)
requirements.testable: Not testable as software. The honest check is commercial: before any institutional build, put the PDF path in front of three institutional buyers and ask what would actually make them switch. If the answer is LMS integration rather than scanning quality, the roadmap is wrong and we should learn that from a conversation rather than from a quarter of engineering.

requirements.complaint: "It only does multiple choice, I still hand-mark everything that matters." The standard structural criticism of the whole category, and the opening that AI-grading entrants are attacking through with handwriting and open-response grading.
requirements.defence: Our defensible position is the exact opposite of theirs and we should say it out loud as a positioning choice rather than leave it as an implementation detail, because the market is about to be very loud with the other claim. Zero ML, entirely on device, deterministic, and provable: the same paper gives the same score, the geometry is printed and known rather than inferred, nothing is uploaded, and the accuracy number comes with a published method. An AI grader can claim more but cannot claim any of that, and in a market whose regulator has already cited weak accuracy as grounds for a ban, provability is worth more than reach. Concretely: make determinism a marketing claim with a number behind it, not a footnote, and resist the first request to add a learned classifier to "improve" bubble detection, because that single change forfeits every sentence above. Where we should extend is toward more question TYPES that remain deterministic (the numeric and short-response designs already sketched in SHEET-SPEC-V3 join QuestionSchema without a migration), not toward inference.
requirements.where: process and positioning, with a standing constraint on the scanner pipeline
requirements.testable: A CI constraint rather than a test: core-omr keeps zero ML dependencies and zero model files, enforced by a dependency allowlist that fails the build on violation. That turns the positioning claim into something a competitor cannot dispute and we cannot quietly abandon.

defences.angle:
Defence engineering: each marking behaviour turned into a mechanism that lives somewhere specific in TransferChecker, with arithmetic from the actual geometry in sheet-spec (radiusMm 2, pitchXMm 5.6, pitchYMm 7, fiducialMm 8, marginMm 6, codeModuleMm 0.5, warp to 1000x1414 on A4 = 4.76 px/mm, so a bubble is 19 px across and 285 px in area).

THE ONE IDEA THAT UNLOCKS MOST OF THE LIST. Section 4 rule 1 says the threshold is relative because absolute thresholds die under shadow. That reasoning was correct given the information the pipeline had. But the sheet already prints its own photometric reference and the pipeline never reads it: four solid 8 mm squares of pure print black at known positions, timing marks of the same ink down the left edge one per row, and paper white guaranteed in the 6 mm margin and in the 1.6 mm gaps between bubbles. Two-point calibration per page, bilinear across the four corners, refined per row by the timing marks, gives every bubble a locally expected black level and white level. Shadow becomes a measured gradient rather than an unknown, and an absolute floor becomes safe. Ten of the fourteen mvp items below either depend on that calibration or get much cheaper with it. It costs one pass over furniture we already print and already find.

THE SECOND STRUCTURAL POINT. Acceptance criterion 8 is right and the runtime rule meant to enforce it does not enforce it. Three consecutive frames from a phone held over a paper share one pose, one exposure and one glare geometry, so a stable near-threshold bubble agrees with itself three times and is accepted. Agreement is standing in for independence. Replace it with two things that are actually deterministic: a decision margin emitted per bubble (how far the ratio sits from the nearest threshold), and frames that differ measurably in pose before their agreement counts for anything. A paper whose every bubble has a large margin is deterministic by construction and needs one frame. A paper with any small margin is not made deterministic by any number of frames, and must be shown to the teacher. That is the same philosophy already written down, applied to the mechanism rather than the outcome.

HONESTY ABOUT THE PLAN SHAPE. Fourteen of twenty below are marked mvp and that is too many for weeks 4 to 6. The critical path is four items, in this order: photometric calibration (1), the absolute ink floor (2), the inset measurement disc (3), and the decision margin with its CI gate (5). Those four are the ones that turn confident wrong answers into flags. If weeks 4 to 6 slip, ship those four and let items 4, 9, 11 land in weeks 7 to 8 alongside the camera, where glare and pose belong anyway. Items 12, 13 and 14 are not engine work at all: 12 is how the golden set is collected, 13 is a policy decision that takes an afternoon and unblocks two screens, 14 is a change to the printed artifact that is nearly free now and a version bump forever after.

WHAT ALSO CAME OUT OF READING THE DOCS AGAINST EACH OTHER. Section 3 promises timing marks so rows are located even when print shifts; the section 4 pipeline goes corners to warp to spec coordinates and never reads them. Section 7 says images are never stored; UI rule 3 shows the teacher the paper image with a verification overlay in review, and competitive note 151 proposes reconciling a rescan by name crop. Those cannot all be true. Both are named as requirements below rather than left to be discovered in week 8.

SOURCING NOTE. The web search budget for this session was exhausted before I could run my own queries, so every external claim below is carried from the citations in the findings brief, attributed to the same URLs. Everything geometric is arithmetic on the repository's own constants and is marked as reasoning. No frequency figure anywhere below is measured; the closed beta in weeks 13 to 14 is the only instrument that could measure one.

requirements.complaint: The app read an empty bubble as an answer on a question the student left completely blank.
requirements.defence: Read the photometric reference the sheet already prints. The four 8 mm fiducials are solid print black at known positions; marginMm 6 and the 1.6 mm inter-bubble gaps are guaranteed paper white; the timing marks give one black sample per question row. Build a bilinear black-level and white-level surface across the page from the four corners, correct it per row from that row's timing mark, and express every bubble's darkness on that normalised scale. This is what makes an absolute floor survivable under the shadow that motivated the relative rule in the first place, and it costs one pass over furniture the contour stage already finds. Seed constants by analogy with OMRChecker, which refuses a local threshold when the spread inside a strip is under MIN_GAP 30 grey levels and only trusts a local jump above MIN_JUMP 25 plus CONFIDENT_SURPLUS 5 (https://github.com/Udayraj123/OMRChecker/blob/master/src/core.py). Ours are a fraction of the measured black-to-white range rather than raw grey levels, because the range is now known per page.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, as a stage between warp and bubble sampling
requirements.testable: Render a sheet through sheet-pdf, composite a synthetic illumination gradient of a known ramp across it (paper white falling from 250 to 120 across the page), and assert that the recovered white-level surface tracks the ramp within 5 percent at every bubble centre, and that the same paper under flat light and under the ramp produces identical normalised darkness per bubble within 0.02.

requirements.complaint: The app read an empty bubble as an answer on a question the student left completely blank.
requirements.defence: An absolute ink floor beneath the relative rule. fill_i / max(fill) has no defined behaviour when every bubble is empty: the denominator becomes the largest piece of noise and the ratios normalise to roughly 1.0, 0.9, 0.9, 0.9, so the top one clears 0.65 with no second above 0.45 and a blank question becomes a confident answer. The sheet makes this worse before the student touches it: at radiusMm 2 with a 0.25 mm printed stroke the outline annulus is about 3.1 mm2 against a 12.57 mm2 disc, so an untouched bubble is already about 25 percent dark, and camera blur dilates it further (reasoning, arithmetic on paper.ts and spec.ts). Rule: a question is scored only when the darkest bubble's absolute normalised coverage clears F_abs and its lead over the runner-up clears G_abs. Below F_abs the question is BLANK, which is a real state, not an answer and not an ambiguity. Seed F_abs at 0.30 measured on the inset disc, consistent with the 30 to 40 percent area figure vendors quote (https://formread.org/blog/exam-tricks), and G_abs at 0.15, then earn both on the golden set. Blank and ambiguous get different words in the UI: blank is the student's decision, ambiguous is our inability.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, as a precondition on the normalisation step in section 4 rule 1
requirements.testable: A golden-set case per choice count where the student answered nothing at all on five questions of a fifty question paper. Assert those five come back BLANK, that no letter is emitted for them, and that the flag is 'blank' not 'ambiguous'. Second test: a synthetic sheet with zero student marks anywhere must score zero with fifty blanks and zero ambiguities, and must do so identically at three simulated exposures.

requirements.complaint: The mark was between two bubbles and the app picked the wrong one, or called it a double. They circled the letter instead of filling the bubble.
requirements.defence: Two geometric changes, both free once the coordinates are known. First, measure fill on a disc inset to 0.75 of the bubble radius: r 1.5 mm, 7.1 px, 160 px of sample area, whose edge clears the inner edge of a 0.25 mm printed outline by 0.375 mm or 1.8 px. That removes the printed outline from the numerator entirely and raises the overshoot a neighbour must make before it contributes at all from 1.6 mm to 2.1 mm, a 31 percent wider tolerance, which matters because pitchXMm 5.6 leaves only 1.6 mm or 7.6 px of white between bubble edges. Second, sample an escape ring from 1.1r to 1.4r, that is 2.2 mm to 2.8 mm from centre, 213 px of area that by construction contains no printed ink and no neighbouring bubble: the nearest neighbour's edge is at 3.6 mm and the row below at 5 mm. Ink in the escape ring means the mark left its bubble, which is exactly the signature of a circled letter, a cross drawn through a bubble, a struck-out answer and rough work. That gets its own flag rather than being folded into the fill ratio. Caveat that the escape ring must be masked on the label side when placement is 'external', because externalLabelMm 3.2 puts printed letter ink inside the ring. All arithmetic is reasoning on paper.ts and spec.ts, not cited.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, sampling geometry, derived in sheet-spec so print and scan cannot drift
requirements.testable: Synthetic marks rendered at controlled offsets: a filled bubble displaced 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm toward its neighbour. Assert the neighbour's inset-disc coverage stays under F_abs until 2.1 mm, and that the escape ring fires at 1.6 mm. Separately, render a ring drawn around the bubble outline and assert it produces escape-ring ink with inset-disc coverage below F_abs, so it is flagged and never scored.

requirements.complaint: The bubbles look silver or white on the camera and the app says it cannot read them, or scores them blank.
requirements.defence: Treat saturation as its own channel, not as darkness. Graphite is a plate-like specular flake, so under a point source a shaded bubble returns a highlight brighter than paper and the fill ratio does not fall, it inverts: the darkest bubble becomes the brightest, and the question then falls into the blank case above, so the two failures compound. Count pixels in the inset disc at or above 0.95 of the locally expected paper white from item 1. If that fraction exceeds about 0.10 of the disc, the bubble's darkness is not trustworthy: reject the whole frame rather than the question, because glare is a property of the pose and the very next frame from a different angle is clean. Frames are already dropped freely by the AsyncRunner in section 4 rule 5, so this costs nothing but a moment. Pair it with two process rules: the torch stays off by default because a point source is the cause, and the live corner overlay gains a third state that says move, not just locked and not locked. Two independent camera-OMR vendors rank this as their single largest cause of misreads, which is the strongest frequency claim in the whole research set and is specific to camera capture (https://support.zipgrade.com/hc/en-us/articles/203172225-What-lighting-conditions-work-best, https://support.allinlearning.com/hc/en-us/articles/200665530-Bubble-Sheet-Scanning-Not-Working-Well-includes-VIDEO).
requirements.where: scanner pipeline for detection, interface for the move instruction, process for torch-off
requirements.testable: Golden set gains at least twenty phone captures under a single directional lamp positioned to glare, with the true answers recorded by hand. Assert none of them produces a wrong scored answer: each must either read correctly or be rejected as a glare frame. Synthetic version for CI without hardware: composite a saturated elliptical blob over a known-shaded bubble and assert the glare flag fires and the frame is refused rather than the bubble read as empty.

requirements.complaint: The same paper scanned twice gave two different scores, two minutes apart.
requirements.defence: Emit a decision margin for every bubble and make it a first-class output alongside the fill ratio, then gate on it. Margin is the distance from the value that decided the bubble to the nearest threshold it could have crossed, on the normalised scale from item 1. A paper whose smallest margin is large is deterministic by construction: no plausible exposure change flips it, and one frame is enough. A paper containing a small margin is not made deterministic by any number of frames. This converts determinism from a property we sample by rescanning into a property we measure on every scan. It also gives CI a far stronger gate than equality on the shots we happen to own: assert that across the golden set the minimum decision margin on any bubble that was silently scored stays above a published floor, so a change that moves the engine closer to a cliff fails even when it does not yet fall off it. This is the direct answer to competitor finding 49, where a bubble sitting in the grey band was decided by whichever way the noise fell (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/zipgrade/id635077270).
requirements.where: scanner pipeline output type, and a CI gate in the golden-set harness
requirements.testable: The per-bubble result type carries margin. CI asserts min margin over all silently scored bubbles across the golden set exceeds the floor, and separately runs a perturbation sweep: re-score every golden image at plus and minus 10 percent exposure and plus and minus 1 px of homography jitter, and assert zero answer changes. Any answer that flips under that sweep is by definition a bubble whose margin was understated, which is a bug in the margin calculation, not in the threshold.

requirements.complaint: The same paper scanned twice gave two different scores, two minutes apart.
requirements.defence: Replace 'three consecutive frames agree' with two conditions that mean what the rule was trying to mean. First, accepted frames must be pose-diverse: agreement only counts between frames whose detected fiducial corners have moved by a measurable amount, or whose mean luma differs measurably, so the three readings are not three copies of one reading with one glare geometry and one exposure. Seed at a mean corner motion of about 10 px at full source resolution or a 3 percent luma difference, then tune on real captures (reasoning, no source). Second, a paper containing any bubble below the margin floor cannot auto-accept regardless of how many frames agree, because that is precisely the bubble that agreement cannot vouch for. Keep the multi-frame requirement for the geometry stage, where fiducial and code decoding genuinely benefit from repeats. Add a patience escape: if the teacher holds still and no pose diversity arrives within about 1.5 seconds, accept when every margin is large, and otherwise show the card, because a hand that will not move is not a reason to guess.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline acceptance logic, surfaced in the interface as the reason a scan has not accepted yet
requirements.testable: Unit test the acceptance state machine against synthetic frame sequences: three identical frames containing one small-margin bubble must not accept; three pose-diverse frames with all margins large must accept on the third; one frame with all margins large and the patience timer expired must accept. Field test in the closed beta: log how often the patience escape fires, because if it fires on most papers the diversity requirement is set too high and is costing the teacher time.

requirements.complaint: The same paper scanned twice gave two different scores, two minutes apart.
requirements.defence: Extend acceptance criterion 8 so determinism covers the flag set, not only the score. As written, three shots of one paper could produce the same total while one shot flags a bubble uncertain and another does not, and the build would pass. That is the same non-determinism wearing a hat, and it is worse for trust than a score difference because the teacher sees a warning appear and disappear. The comparison across a paper's shots is on the full result: the answer string, the blank set, the ambiguous set, the uncertain-bubble set, the glare and escape flags, and the id read state. Any difference fails the build, exactly as criterion 8 already says for the score.
requirements.where: process, as an amendment to acceptance criterion 8 and to the golden-set harness
requirements.testable: The golden-set harness serialises the entire result object per shot and diffs shots of the same paper. The test that proves the test works: deliberately introduce a one-grey-level exposure change into a golden paper's second shot and confirm the harness catches a flag-set difference it would previously have passed.

requirements.complaint: The student shaded it, just faintly, and the machine gave them a zero. They only coloured a crescent of it.
requirements.defence: The relative rule already handles the uniformly light student, and it handles a single partial fill well: 0.4 absolute against three empties at 0.2 normalises to 1.0 against 0.5 and fires correctly. The exposure is volume, not wrongness. A second partial fill in the same question, say 0.4 and 0.25, normalises to 1.0 and 0.63 and trips the runner-up clause on a question whose intent a human reads instantly. If the grey band flags one question in ten across thirty papers the teacher stops trusting the flag, and the safety mechanism is trained out of use, which is a worse outcome than the errors it prevents. So make flag rate a first-class CI metric with its own budget alongside the 99.7 percent accuracy gate: a PR that raises accuracy by flagging more fails. Seed the budget at 2 percent of questions and 10 percent of papers touched by any flag, then set it honestly from the beta. This is the discipline that keeps 'never guess' from degrading into 'always ask'.
requirements.where: process, as a second CI gate in the golden-set harness, and interface in how flags are grouped for review
requirements.testable: CI computes flag rate per category (blank, ambiguous, uncertain, glare, escape, changed-answer, id) over the golden set and fails the build if the total exceeds the budget, printing the per-category breakdown so a regression names itself. Report accuracy and flag rate together in every CI summary so neither can be improved silently at the other's expense.

requirements.complaint: They erased it but you can still see it, and the app counted both.
requirements.defence: Give an erasure ghost its own band and its own meaning. On the normalised scale from item 1 an erased bubble is a low-contrast disc at roughly 0.10 to 0.35 coverage, and the destructive case is a 0.3 ghost beside a 0.9 fresh mark: read correctly nine times and wrongly the tenth, which is exactly competitor finding 49. Three parts. First, the grey band must extend down far enough to see a ghost, so a band spanning only 0.45 to 0.65 of the normalised ratio is too narrow at the bottom and would drop a 0.3 ghost silently. Second, a ghost is directional information, not noise: one bubble above F_abs plus one bubble in the ghost band, where the fresh mark leads by a documented discrimination margin, is a CHANGED ANSWER, a different event from a genuine double at 0.9 and 0.85, and it gets different words in the UI. Third, name the constants. Scantron ships Mark Threshold as Light, Normal, Dark and a Discrimination Margin on a 3 to 15 scale; Remark ships a separate Erasure Threshold feeding changed-answer reporting (https://www.scantron.com/ScanToolsPlus/Help/v8/STXAppl/content/appdevcontent/80_topics/popups/read_controls_-_discrimination_margin.htm, https://remarksoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Remark-Office-OMR-Users-Guide11.pdf). Our 0.65 and 0.45 are that knob welded shut and currently living as two literals in a pipeline comment. They become named, documented, tested constants with a written rationale, whether or not we ever expose them to a teacher.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline for detection, interface for the changed-answer wording, sheet-spec for where the constants live
requirements.testable: Synthetic ghosts rendered at 0.10, 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 coverage beside a 0.90 fresh mark. Assert every one of them is seen, that none of them silently produces a double, and that the classification is changed-answer rather than ambiguous when the fresh mark leads by the margin. Then the harder test, which is the whole point: three captures of each ghost case at different exposures must produce identical classification.

requirements.complaint: The student filled in only half their ID number.
requirements.defence: Three states, not two. Section 4 rule 9 defines complete and unset and correctly refuses the competitor's silent ID: 0, but a grid with three of six columns shaded is neither, and under the current rule it resolves to whichever branch the code happens to take, most likely a malformed id string with placeholder characters, which is the invented value the rule exists to forbid. Define complete, partial and absent. Partial carries which columns read and which did not, and is shown next to the name crop, because a human reading the handwritten name resolves in one second what the grid cannot. The consequence that matters most is reconciliation: rule 8 matches a rescan on same template and same student id, and a partial id read slightly differently on two passes will silently fail to match and produce exactly the duplicate record acceptance criterion 9 promises to prevent. So the rule is that a partial id never auto-matches. It always goes to the teacher with both candidates and the two name crops side by side. No source found for this complaint anywhere in the research; it is adjacent to competitive note 43 and is reasoning.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline for the read, interface for the resolution, database for the stored state
requirements.testable: Automated test scanning a paper whose id grid has columns 1, 2 and 4 shaded: assert the state is partial, that no id string is emitted, and that no auto-match occurs. Then extend the acceptance criterion 9 test: scan the same partial-id paper twice and assert the record count stays at one only after the teacher chooses, and that the app never chose for them.

requirements.complaint: The sheet came back folded and the fold ran right through the answers, and the printer shifted the whole grid down a couple of millimetres.
requirements.defence: Actually read the timing marks. Section 3 prints one per question row precisely so a row is located even when print shifts, and the section 4 pipeline goes corners to warp to spec coordinates and never touches them, so the promise is printed on the paper and unimplemented in the engine. Place each row from its own timing mark and interpolate only where a mark is missing. This recovers the drift a crease introduces, which matters because a single global homography from four corners cannot flatten a non-planar page and the inter-bubble gap is only 7.6 px, so a drift of one or two pixels is a real fraction of the margin for error. It also doubles as the per-row black reference in item 1, so the same read serves two purposes. What timing marks do not fix is the crease shadow itself: under directional light a crease is a hard line that adaptiveThreshold with blockSize 25 renders as black pixels inside every bubble it crosses, raising a whole row's coverage together. Relative normalisation cancels a shadow that lifts a whole question uniformly, which is a genuine strength worth stating; it does not cancel one that crosses two bubbles of five.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, as a row-registration stage after warp
requirements.testable: Synthetic sheets rendered with the question grid displaced 1, 2 and 3 mm vertically relative to the fiducials, plus a rendered crease shadow across rows 12 to 14. Assert row centres are recovered within 1 px in every case, and assert that the crease rows either read correctly or flag, never score wrongly. Real-paper version: at least fifteen golden-set papers physically folded, captured by phone under directional light, since a flatbed will not reproduce the shadow at all.

requirements.complaint: They pressed so hard you can feel it on the back of the page. The eraser wore a shiny thin patch. The bubbles glared silver.
requirements.defence: None of these classes exist for a flatbed scanner, which illuminates diffusely, and all of them exist for a phone. An indentation trough under a single off-axis source gives a bright rim and a dark shadow line that adaptiveThreshold turns into black pixels; a burnished erasure patch is smoother than surrounding paper and produces the same specular inversion as graphite; a thinned patch is translucent so a duplex sheet shows through. Section 13 is right that the engine should be proven on flatbed scans first, and the consequence nobody has written down is that a golden set built mainly that way makes this entire class structurally invisible to CI. So the golden set gets a composition quota, not just a count: of the 300-plus papers, at least 40 percent captured by phone; within those, at least 30 under a single directional source, at least 20 non-flat (folded, curled or on an uneven surface), at least 20 deliberately glared, at least 15 carrying heavy erasures, and zero captured with the torch on. Every paper keeps its minimum three shots per criterion 8, and shots of one paper must differ in pose and lighting or they do not count as three. The literature does not cover this: nothing was found on indentation, burnishing or crease shadow under camera capture, so our golden set is the primary source and should be treated as an asset, which also feeds the published-numbers strategy in section 8b.
requirements.where: process, as the definition of the golden set that everything else is measured against
requirements.testable: The harness refuses to report an accuracy number if the quota is unmet, and prints the current composition against the quota on every run. That is the test: a metric measured on the wrong instrument is not a metric, and the harness should say so rather than print 99.8 percent from 300 flatbed scans.

requirements.complaint: I wanted to check the machine's marking against the paper, and I wanted a rescan to find the paper I scanned yesterday.
requirements.defence: Resolve a contradiction between three of our own documents before week 8 builds on the wrong side of it. Section 7 says paper images are never uploaded and never stored and are deleted immediately, which is our strongest privacy claim and a real cost advantage at 26 riyals a year. UI rule 3 shows the teacher the paper image with a green and red verification overlay in review, and competitive note 151 proposes reconciling a rescan against an existing record by name crop. Neither is possible if the image is gone the moment the frame is released, and neither is possible across sessions. The resolution that keeps the promise intact: what is never uploaded and never leaves the device is the rule, and what persists locally is a bounded, named artifact in the encrypted SQLCipher database. Concretely, retain the name crop, which at a medium written box of 52 by 10 mm is about 248 by 48 px and a few kilobytes, plus optionally a downscaled warped page for review, both device-only, both never synced, both deleted on a documented schedule and on exam deletion. Write it down as a numbered rule with the same weight as the others, because the wrong reading of section 7 silently kills the review screen and rescan reconciliation, and the wrong reading of UI rule 3 silently kills the privacy claim.
requirements.where: process for the policy, database for retention, interface for review and reconciliation
requirements.testable: An automated test asserts that no sync payload ever contains image bytes, of any size, from any table. A second asserts the local name crop survives an app restart and is found by the reconciliation path. A third asserts deleting an exam removes every crop belonging to it. The privacy claim is then something we can prove in a sentence rather than something we hope stayed true.

requirements.complaint: They did their working out on the answer sheet and drew all over it, and the sheet printed at 94 percent so nothing scanned.
requirements.defence: Three cheap changes to the printed artifact, which are nearly free now and a version bump forever after, since paper.ts states plainly that these constants are part of the printed artifact. First, print an explicit rough-work zone and declare the margins off limits in the same band as the existing 100 percent scale warning, because a doodle inside a bubble costs one flagged question while a doodle touching an 8 mm fiducial or a 6 by 3 mm timing mark costs the whole page, and the left margin is exactly where a right-hander's working lands. Vendors treat rough work as a named offence for this reason (https://www.addmengroup.com/omr-filling/rough-work-on-omr-sheet.htm). Second, correct our own understanding of fit-to-page: uniform shrink is largely harmless, because the homography maps the four measured fiducial centres onto the canonical rectangle and the scale cancels exactly, which is a real architectural strength worth stating rather than a risk. What fit-to-page actually destroys is the printed code, since codeModuleMm 0.5 is documented as the floor at which a phone stops resolving modules and a 94 percent print puts it at 0.47 mm. So give the module size headroom and, third, make the failure speak: when all four fiducials lock and the code does not decode, the message is not 'cannot read' but 'the code did not read, check that you printed at 100 percent and not Fit to Page'. All arithmetic is reasoning on paper.ts.
requirements.where: sheet design in sheet-spec and sheet-pdf, interface for the failure message
requirements.testable: Render every stock template at 100, 96, 94 and 90 percent, capture or synthesise each, and assert the decode-failure message names the print scale rather than a generic failure. Separately, render sheets with a scribble crossing one fiducial and with a scribble crossing three timing marks, and assert the corner overlay tells the teacher which corner, and that the timing-mark case degrades to interpolation rather than failing the page.

requirements.complaint: They ticked the box instead of shading it, or put an X. They used pen, crossed out the wrong answer and filled a different one.
requirements.defence: One morphology operation separates a shading from a stroke. Erode the bubble's dark mask by 1 px and take the ratio of surviving area: a filled disc of radius 7.1 px keeps (6.1/7.1)^2 or about 74 percent, while a ballpoint stroke under 2 px wide after warp keeps essentially nothing (reasoning, arithmetic on spec.ts at 4.76 px/mm). That single descriptor separates shaded from tick, cross, circle, crease shadow and eraser crumb, with no ML and full determinism. It matters most for the cross-out, which is the one behaviour where a naive fill ratio gets the answer exactly backwards: a struck-out bubble has MORE dark area than a filled one, so it ranks first, becomes the denominator, and pushes the student's real answer below 0.65. Both GradeCam and Gradescope name this case and neither tries to resolve it; Gradescope refuses it outright (https://support.gradecam.com/hc/en-us/articles/13962088292635-Troubleshooting-Best-Practices, https://guides.gradescope.com/hc/en-us/articles/22065675043341-Grading-a-Bubble-Sheet-Assignment). We do not resolve it either; we detect it and say 'marked but not shaded' or 'struck through', which is a flag the teacher can act on in a second rather than a silent blank or a silent inversion. This is after-mvp because the escape ring in item 3 already catches the cases whose strokes leave the bubble, which is most cross-outs and every circled letter; erosion survival adds the marks that stay entirely inside.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, as a second descriptor returned per bubble alongside the fill ratio
requirements.testable: Synthetic marks rendered per class: solid fill, 60 percent crescent, centred dot, tick, X, circle around the outline, a 1 px shadow line across the bubble, and a struck-through fill. Assert erosion survival separates the solid and crescent classes from the stroke classes with a gap of at least 0.4, at three simulated blur levels. Then assert the classifier never converts a stroke class into a scored answer.

requirements.complaint: They used a green gel pen and half the sheet came back blank, or every question came back flagged.
requirements.defence: Add chroma as a second ink channel and do it in the space the camera already gives us. A mid-red at roughly 30 percent luma reads as grey after greyscale conversion, so a red-filled bubble can sit at coverage 0.4 to 0.6 and land in the grey band on every single question, turning the paper into a wall of flags. The frame arrives as YUV, so chroma magnitude sqrt((U-128)^2 + (V-128)^2) is free: coloured ink has high chroma, paper and graphite have near zero. Define ink as the maximum of luma darkness and a scaled chroma magnitude, seeded around a chroma threshold of 25, which makes a red or green mark as dark as a pencil one without an RGB conversion (reasoning, no source; the underlying claim that coloured pens lose contrast in greyscale is from https://www.addmengroup.com/omr-filling/colour-of-pen-for-filling-omr.htm). Note the genuine strength here and measure it rather than assume it: because our threshold normalises within a question, a consistently red-marking student already survives better than an absolute-threshold system would. Also note the one place ballpoint helps us, since it is darker and glare-immune compared to graphite; its cost is that it cannot be erased, which pushes students into the cross-out behaviour above.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, at the point where the frame is reduced to a single ink channel
requirements.testable: Golden-set papers filled in red, green, blue and black ink and in HB pencil, same answers on all five. Assert identical answer strings across all five, and assert flag rate on the coloured papers stays inside the same budget as the pencil ones. That second assertion is the real test, because passing on accuracy while flagging every question is a failure wearing a pass.
