requirements.complaint: They skipped a question, went on, and every answer after that was one row out.
requirements.defence: Not a detection failure at all, which is why no imaging work will ever catch it and why it belongs in the scoring layer. Every bubble reads perfectly; the paper genuinely says what we read. But the signature is visible for free in data we already store: a run of correct answers, then a long tail near chance, and a trailing blank. At scoring time, re-score the stored answer string against the key at shift 0, +1 and -1, and if a shifted score exceeds the actual by a wide margin while the actual sits near chance, raise 'this paper scores much higher shifted by one row, review it'. Costs O(questions x 3) on strings already in scans.answers, needs no image, and therefore runs retroactively on papers graded weeks ago and even at class level, where several papers showing it at once points at the key rather than the students. Test-prep sources call this the single most damaging bubble-sheet error precisely because one behaviour destroys a whole paper (https://www.leadingtuition.co.uk/blog/11-answer-sheet-practice-how-to-fill-in-bubble-sheets-and-avoid-costly-mistakes). No competitor in our notes offers it. It fits the stated philosophy exactly: do not correct it, show the teacher.
requirements.where: scoring, on stored answer strings, surfaced in the interface as a review prompt
requirements.testable: Pure unit tests, no images: generate answer strings from a key with a deliberate shift injected at question k for k across the paper, and assert detection above a stated sensitivity with a false-positive rate under a stated ceiling on unshifted papers, measured over the whole golden set's real answer strings. The false-positive number is the one that decides whether this ships.

requirements.complaint: They circled the letter instead of filling the bubble, and the same behaviour broke differently on two of our own sheets.
requirements.defence: One student behaviour, three failure signatures, chosen by a field the teacher picks in the builder, and this is not currently written down anywhere. With placement 'internal', our default, the letter is inside the bubble, so a circling student draws a ring on or just outside the printed outline: not blank, but a partial annulus adding roughly 0.15 to 0.3 of coverage, which is the grey band. With 'header' the letters live once above the column and the bubbles are empty, so the student circles a header letter belonging to no question and every question reads blank. With 'external' the letter sits beside its bubble in externalLabelMm 3.2, so the circle lands in the inter-bubble gap and may clip two bubbles, and it is also why the escape ring from item 3 must be masked on the label side for this placement. Two consequences: a line of copy in the sheet builder telling the teacher what each placement trades, and three separate golden-set cases rather than one, because a fix validated on 'internal' proves nothing about the other two.
requirements.where: sheet design for the builder copy, scanner pipeline for the placement-aware escape ring, process for the golden-set cases
requirements.testable: Three golden-set papers, one per placement, with the same student circling letters rather than shading. Assert none produces a scored answer, that each produces a flag, and that the flag text differs usefully between them. Assert the escape ring is masked for 'external' by rendering a clean 'external' sheet with no student marks at all and confirming the ring reads zero ink rather than picking up the printed letters.

requirements.complaint: The student used one of those erasable pens and parts of the sheet had faded by the time I scanned it.
requirements.defence: Mostly not our problem today, and that is worth understanding rather than dismissing. Pilot states FriXion ink becomes colourless above about 140F and that the pens must not be used for exams or official documents (https://www.pilot-frixion.uk/uk/frequently-asked-questions/). Because we process on-device from a phone photo taken minutes after the exam, we skip the heat exposure that destroys these marks in a document feeder or copier. That flips into a genuine risk on the phase-two institutional path in competitive note 36, where a warm scanner lamp and feed rollers can erase the paper as it is read, producing the worst possible determinism failure: the paper itself changed between passes, so a re-scan of a stored stack loses answers and nothing in our engine did anything wrong. Response now: one line in the printed instructions. Response then: a documented known-limitation for the PDF and document-scanner route, so institutions hear it from us before they discover it. Watch rather than build, because the mitigation is words until the scanner route exists.
requirements.where: sheet design for the printed line, process for the phase-two limitation note
requirements.testable: Nothing to test in software today. When the PDF route ships, the check is a manual one done once: a FriXion-marked sheet through a real document feeder, photographed before and after, to confirm or refute the mechanism on the hardware institutions actually use, and the answer goes in the docs either way.

requirements.complaint: The eraser wore a thin patch and the answer on the back showed through.
requirements.defence: Default to single-sided sheets, and if duplex is ever offered, offset the reverse side's grid so a bubble never sits directly behind a bubble. A scrubbed patch is thinner and more translucent, so on a duplex sheet the reverse mark shows through as grey inside the bubble, and eraser crumbs left behind are opaque specks in arbitrary positions (https://www.addmengroup.com/omr-filling/how-to-erase-on-omr-sheet.htm). The offset is a pure layout change costing nothing, and it turns a bleed-through into ink landing on white paper where the escape ring sees it as an anomaly rather than the disc seeing it as an answer. Related and cheap: a real shading is smooth while crumbs and residue are speckled, so quadrant spread or interior variance separates them, which is the same family of descriptor as item 15 and should be built at the same time rather than separately. Watch rather than mvp because our small paper sizes already exist so that several sheets tile one page without scaling, which reduces the pressure to print duplex in the first place.
requirements.where: sheet design in sheet-pdf layout, scanner pipeline for the speckle descriptor
requirements.testable: Print one duplex sheet with heavy shading on both sides and one single-sided, photograph both under the same light, and compare coverage on bubbles that sit back to back against ones that do not. If the difference is under the margin floor from item 5, this stays a watch item permanently and we say so in the docs instead of carrying it as open work.

defences.alreadyCovered:
Named so we do not congratulate ourselves twice, with the nuance where the existing decision is nearly right rather than fully right.

FULLY ANSWERED ALREADY, no new work:
- Two shaded bubbles scored wrong with no warning. Section 4 rule 2 stops and shows the teacher, and the live counter in 'what is measured and shown at every scan' puts it on screen with the paper still in the teacher's hand. That is better than the market: FormRead describes the commercial norm as recording multiple answers and marking the question wrong automatically with no review (https://formread.org/blog/exam-tricks).
- Check-all-that-apply misread as an error. select: 'many' in spec.ts makes the sheet self-describing, so the scanner knows the difference without holding the key. This is a genuine structural advantage and nothing in the research suggested a competitor has it.
- Shadow across the page, and the uniformly light-shading student. Section 4 rule 1. The relative rule handles both correctly and item 1 above only extends its reach, it does not replace it.
- A palm smear that lifts a whole question together. Relative normalisation cancels common-mode lift because it raises numerator and denominator alike. Worth stating explicitly as a strength rather than leaving it implicit, since it is real and unearned credit is not what this is; the case it does not cancel is a smear covering two bubbles of five.
- A consistently coloured pen across the whole paper. Per-question normalisation survives it far better than an absolute threshold would. Item 16 is about the mixed and grey-band cases, not this one.
- ID: 0 invented from an empty grid. Section 4 rule 9 already refuses the exact defect at competitive note 43. Item 10 adds only the third state, partial.
- A rescan making a second contradictory record. Section 4 rule 8 and acceptance criterion 9 already cover it, with an automated test. Item 10 only notes that a partial id defeats the match key.
- Handwriting the machine cannot read. The name crop is already specified and already has its geometry: usage 'studentName' plus WrittenBoxLayout.box. Competitive note 40 called this our strongest confirmation and it stands.
- The teacher not knowing why a sheet will not read. UI rule 1's per-corner feedback is exactly the right affordance and items 4 and 14 extend it rather than invent it.
- Folded paper appearing in the golden set at all. Section 4 already lists it. Item 12 changes how the set is captured, not whether folds are in it.
- Printing at the wrong scale. The printed warning exists in section 3, and item 14 corrects our own understanding of what fit-to-page actually breaks.
- Small sheets scanning badly because they were shrunk. paper.ts already refuses this by designing A5 and A6 at true size and tiling rather than scaling. That decision is correct and load-bearing.

RIGHT IN INTENT, INCOMPLETE IN MECHANISM, which is where items 2, 5, 6 and 11 land:
- Section 4 rule 1's relative threshold is correct for shadow and has no defined behaviour on an all-blank question. Item 2.
- Section 4 rule 6's fill ratio not boolean is correct and stops one step short: the ratio is emitted, the distance from the threshold is not, and the distance is what predicts determinism. Item 5.
- Section 4 rule 3's three consecutive frames is aimed at the right target and uses agreement as a proxy for independence. Item 6.
- Section 3's timing marks are printed on the paper and never read by the section 4 pipeline. Item 11.
- Acceptance criterion 8 is the right criterion and covers the score but not the flag set. Item 7.
defences.cannotDefend:
Five things no software can fix, and what we do anyway. The theme is that refusing clearly is a feature, and refusing at the right moment, with the paper still in the teacher's hand, is most of the product.

1. A GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS MARK HAS NO CORRECT READING. Two bubbles at 0.50 and 0.45 do not contain an answer. No threshold, no model and no number of frames recovers information the paper does not hold; anything that returns a letter there has invented it. What we do: refuse in under 400 ms, name the question and circle the bubble on the paper image, and let the teacher decide in the same screen without leaving scan mode. Measure the refusal, not just the accuracy: a flag the teacher resolves in two seconds is a feature and a flag they learn to dismiss is a defect, which is why the flag-rate budget in item 8 sits in CI beside the 99.7 percent gate. The competitor's App Store reviews contradict each other, one saying erasures are read as second answers and another saying deliberate smudges and partial fills all scored correctly (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/zipgrade/id635077270). Both can be true at different poses, and that non-determinism is the thing we are actually selling against.

2. A ROW-SHIFTED PAPER IS CORRECTLY READ AND WRONGLY ANSWERED. The student put their answers in the wrong rows. We read exactly what is there, the score is right by the key, and the grade is wrong by intent. Nothing in imaging touches this. What we do: item 17, a free shift check on stored strings that says 'this paper scores far better shifted by one, look at it', and then stops. We never rescore it.

3. A PAPER THAT HAS PHYSICALLY CHANGED. FriXion ink faded by heat, a torn sheet, a bubble scrubbed through to a hole, working-out inked over a fiducial. The information left the paper before the camera arrived. What we do: refuse rather than guess, say which corner or which region failed so the teacher can act, and accept that the answer is sometimes to transfer the marks to a fresh sheet or enter that one paper by hand, which is what every vendor's guidance says too (https://www.addmengroup.com/OMR-Filling/how-to-handle-omr-sheets.htm). One manually entered paper in a stack of thirty is a good outcome; one silently wrong paper is not.

4. STUDENT AND TEACHER BEHAVIOUR. We cannot make a student shade fully, keep to HB, avoid the margins, or bring a pencil at all; we cannot make a teacher print at 100 percent, work under diffuse light, or hold the phone at a different angle. What we do: put the instruction on the paper where the student is looking (rough-work zone, marking instruction, the existing 100 percent warning), and make the app ask for the one change that fixes the current frame at the moment it matters, which for glare is 'move' and not 'error'. Two vendors independently rank glare as their largest cause of misreads and both prescribe moving (https://support.zipgrade.com/hc/en-us/articles/203172225-What-lighting-conditions-work-best, https://support.allinlearning.com/hc/en-us/articles/200665530-Bubble-Sheet-Scanning-Not-Working-Well-includes-VIDEO). A printed warning nobody reads is not a defence; a live instruction at the moment of failure is.

5. WE DO NOT KNOW THE BASE RATES, AND NOBODY DOES. The research found no study, vendor figure or exam-board statistic giving the fraction of real classroom questions that are double-marked, lightly filled, ghosted or ticked. Every vendor asserts these matter; none publishes a denominator. So every threshold below is seeded by analogy and must be earned on our own data, and nobody should quote a frequency from this work as measured. What we do: instrument the closed beta in weeks 13 to 14 to log the flag reason per question, anonymously and on-device, and treat the resulting distribution as the artifact. Twenty teachers times a few hundred papers is the only instrument that exists for this question, it costs almost nothing to build while the beta is happening anyway, and the published result feeds directly into the section 8b argument that our real measured numbers are the discoverability advantage. The gap in the literature is an opportunity, not just a caveat.

A SIXTH, ABOUT OUR OWN TOOLING RATHER THAN THE WORLD. The golden set needs 300 real papers we do not have, which STATUS.md already names as the risk that could stall weeks 4 to 6. Almost every test above is written against synthetic marks composited onto sheets rendered by sheet-pdf, which we already have in docs/samples: controlled shadow ramps, specular blobs, ghosts at chosen densities, strokes at chosen widths, geometric displacements. That is not a substitute for real paper and it will not prove 99.7 percent, but it is enough to prove that each named defence fires, and it can exist before a single real photograph does. Build the synthetic mark renderer first; it is the thing that lets the engine be written while the paper is being collected.

defences.angle:
Capture defence, written against our own constants rather than against generic OMR advice. Three framings shape the list.

First, a correction that came out of reading the pipeline in PLAN.md section 4 next to the numbers in paper.ts. The pipeline reads: frame → resize ×0.25 → threshold → contours → four points → getPerspectiveTransform → warp to 1000×1414 → decode code → sample bubbles. If the homography is fitted on the quarter-scale image and the warp is fed from that same quarter-scale image, then on a 1080p frame with the sheet filling it we are sampling a page at roughly 0.84 px/mm, where a 4 mm bubble is 3.4 px across and a 0.5 mm code module is 0.42 px. Warping that up to 1000×1414 does not restore what was thrown away. The quarter-scale frame is for FINDING the sheet and for nothing else; the homography must be scaled back by 4 and every measurement, the code decode, the fill ratios and the timing marks, must be taken from the full-resolution frame. This is one line of intent and it is load-bearing for the whole engine.

Second, acceptance criterion 8 measures repeatability, and several real conditions produce a stable wrong answer that satisfies it. A dust speck on ADF glass prints the same line at the same x on every page of the batch and on every rescan. A ceiling light reflected off a shiny desk sits in the same place in all three frames. A copier that shrinks every page shrinks them identically. All three pass "three frames agree" and pass "the same paper twice gives the same result" while being wrong. Determinism is a necessary condition, not the guarantee. Agreement between frames should be the tie-breaker after each frame has independently passed a physical-plausibility gate, not the evidence that the reading is right.

Third, our headline rule, fill_i / max(fill) within a question, defends against illumination that varies slowly across the page and is defeated by illumination that varies sharply within one question row. A specular highlight on one bubble, a hard shadow edge crossing a row, a flicker band, a scanner dust line: each changes the ratio between bubbles of the same question, which is exactly the quantity we normalise by. Rule 1 is correct and should be kept; it needs a fence around the cases where its assumption is false, and that fence is per-row.

Underneath most of this list is one instrument we have already printed and are currently under-using. The timing marks are described in grid.ts as row indexing. They are also a geometry proof: they give one measured y per question row, so predicted-versus-measured residuals down the page catch page curl, rolling-shutter shear, lens distortion, scanner transport stretch and photocopy row-pitch drift with a single mechanism, all of which are failures where four corner squares are found cleanly and the warp still lands the sampling discs off the printed bubbles in the middle of the page. That one test is the highest-value item here.

requirements.complaint: The page was curled, or I moved the phone while it read, or the scanner stretched the page, and the grade came out wrong with no warning at all.
requirements.defence: Promote the timing marks from row indexing to a geometry proof. After warping, predict every timing mark centre from the spec, measure where each actually landed, and fit the residual down the page. A flat page correctly warped gives residuals that are small and random; page curl gives a smooth bow; rolling shutter gives a monotonic shear; scanner transport stretch gives row pitch that drifts down the page while all four corners still register perfectly. Concrete budget: the standard warp is 1000 px / 210 mm = 4.76 px/mm, a bubble is radius 2 mm so 19 px across, and a sampling disc still sits safely inside its printed bubble while the row centre error stays under about 1 mm, which is 4.8 px. Refuse at max residual > 0.8 mm, and refuse separately when per-row pitch deviates more than 3% from the pitch the code carries. Sensitivity is not the problem: a 3 mm timing mark is 14 px tall in the warp and its centroid is measurable to roughly 0.2 mm. This single test covers four separate physical failures, all of which are invisible to a four-corner homography because a four-point transform is exact for a plane and only for a plane.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, using geometry the sheet already prints
requirements.testable: Synthesise from clean golden images: a cylindrical warp at known amplitudes (0.5, 1, 2, 4 mm of bow), a shear at known angles, and a vertical stretch of 1%, 2%, 5%. Assert that below the gate the grade is unchanged and above the gate the engine refuses. Separately assert the inverse: that grading these images without the gate changes at least one answer, so the test proves the gate is earning its place.

requirements.complaint: A student wrote next to the black marks down the side, or a corner was dog-eared, and the whole paper scored confidently and wrongly.
requirements.defence: Count the marks, and match them to predictions rather than indexing by ordinal position. The row count is known from the spec, so 'expected 40 timing marks, found 39' is a named refusal, not a silent re-indexing of every row below the damage. Match each found mark to its predicted y by nearest neighbour with a maximum distance of half the row pitch, so a missing mark leaves a hole rather than shifting the whole column by one. This matters because a silent off-by-one is the single worst failure the product can produce: it does not degrade a grade, it invents an entire paper's worth of answers with full confidence. University exam offices already warn students in print that pencil marks over the timing bars cause an exam to be rejected (https://ro.umich.edu/sites/default/files/2020-08/exam-scoring-guide_FA20_0.pdf), which tells us both that the failure is real and that rejection is the accepted answer to it.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline
requirements.testable: Take golden images and paint out timing mark 1, mark 20 and mark 40 in turn, then smudge one with a grey blob. Assert refusal with the edge-damage reason in all four cases, and specifically assert that the engine never returns a full answer string shifted by one row. Add the smudge case to the golden set permanently.

requirements.complaint: I did set 100% in the print dialog and it still will not scan, or my colleague photocopied my master and half the class reads badly.
requirements.defence: Trust nothing we asked the teacher to do; measure the printed artefact. The four fiducial centres give the true printed scale on both axes. On A4 with margin 6 and fiducial 8, centre-to-centre is 210 - 2×10 = 190 mm horizontally and 277 mm vertically, which is 905 px in the warp, so a 1% scale error is 9 px and even 0.3% is measurable from solid-square centroids. Compare against the geometry carried in the printed code and refuse above 1.5% uniform error, reporting the measured number: 'this sheet printed at 94% of its intended size, reprint with scaling off'. Refuse separately above 0.7% anisotropy between the axes, which is the signature of a copier or a transport-speed problem rather than a print-dialog problem. This is necessary because the warning we print cannot be enforced at the point it matters: Adobe documents that 'if your printer applies additional scaling that is not communicated to Acrobat by the printer driver, those scaling factors are applied too' (https://helpx.adobe.com/acrobat/kb/scale-or-resize-printed-pages.html), so a teacher who does everything right can still be defeated by a driver. The OMRChecker maintainer measured shifts of up to 10 px between PDF-printed and photocopied sheets (https://github.com/Udayraj123/OMRChecker/issues/196), which is the same failure arriving by a different route.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, checked against the printed code
requirements.testable: Render one template's PDF at 90, 94, 96, 98, 100, 102 and 105 percent and at 100% with 2% horizontal-only stretch, print or simulate each, and assert the engine reports the true percentage within 0.5 points and refuses everything outside the gate. Then photocopy a real printed sheet on an office machine, first and second generation, and add both to the golden set with the requirement that they are either graded correctly or refused, never graded wrongly.

requirements.complaint: I printed the sheets and the app cannot find the corners, and separately, the black bars down the left edge sit right against the printed site name.
requirements.defence: Two changes to paper.ts, one breaking change and one version bump, and they must land before any sheet exists in the field. First, marginMm 6 to 10. A fiducial's outer edge currently sits 6 mm from the paper edge, while consumer laser printers reserve roughly 4.23 mm on A4 and HP documents a 5 mm unprintable bottom band (https://www.thelasttech.com/post/printer-print-close-to-edge); 6 mm clears a good printer by under 2 mm and does not clear a bad one, and the bottom pair is most at risk. Gradescope makes clipped corner marks its first troubleshooting item (https://teaching.pitt.edu/resources/gradescope-bubble-sheets/). The cost is honest: contentLeftMm goes from 20 to 24 and A4 usable width drops from about 170 to 162 mm, which at pitchXMm 5.6 is roughly one bubble column in the worst layout. Second, the timing column needs a keep-out. Today contentLeftMm = marginMm 6 + timingWidthMm 6 + brandingBandMm 8, so the vertical branding text starts at exactly the millimetre the timing marks end, with zero gap, while Remark's form-design rule asks for no printed lines within 3/8 inch, 9.5 mm, of bubbles. Move branding to the right edge beside the title band or into the 12 mm warning band, and reserve at least 4 mm of clear paper beside every timing mark.
requirements.where: sheet design (paper.ts GEOMETRY, SheetSpec version 3 to 4)
requirements.testable: A pure geometric unit test over the layout output: assert no drawn rectangle of any kind intersects a 4 mm dilation of any timing mark rect, on every stock template and on a fuzzed set of specs. For the margin, crop 5 mm from each edge of rendered sheets to simulate a printer with a large unprintable band, and assert the engine reports cut corner marks rather than a generic failure.

requirements.complaint: It just says it cannot read the sheet and I have no idea what to change.
requirements.defence: Make core-omr return a discriminated union of named outcomes, never a boolean and never a generic failure. The competitor's answer to this problem was to hand the teacher a 'Required Image Sharpness' slider and tell them to drag it left until the sheet is picked up (https://support.zipgrade.com/hc/en-us/articles/201493965-ZipGrade-isn-t-recognizing-an-answer-sheet-It-won-t-scan), which trades silent misreads for a stuck scan and puts a threshold in the hands of someone with no way to reason about it. Ours names the physical condition instead: glare on a bubble, too dark, out of focus, moving, page not flat, printed at the wrong scale, corner mark cut off, edge mark missing or covered, too far away to read the sheet code, dust line down the page, bitonal scan. Every reason is a sentence a teacher can act on in ten seconds, and every reason gets an ar and an en string. Our live corner-lock feedback already covers the case where four corners are not found; this vocabulary covers the much more dangerous set where four corners ARE found and the reading is still not trustworthy. Scope honestly: five or six reasons exist at MVP because only those detectors exist, and the union grows as the rest ship.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline contract, surfaced in the interface
requirements.testable: One golden-set fixture per reason code, asserting the engine returns exactly that code. A CI check that every reason in the union has an ar and an en translation key and that no reason string uses an em dash. In closed beta with 20 teachers, log which reason codes fire and how often a teacher rescans successfully after seeing each one; a reason that never leads to a successful rescan is a badly worded reason.

requirements.complaint: The bubbles look shiny in the photo and a filled bubble was read as empty.
requirements.defence: ZipGrade states that glare reflecting off pencil marks 'has historically caused more mismarks than any other problem' (https://support.zipgrade.com/hc/en-us/articles/203172225-What-lighting-conditions-work-best), and GradeCam says pencils 'can reflect more light and make it more difficult to discern student responses' (https://support.gradecam.com/hc/en-us/articles/13962088292635-Troubleshooting-Best-Practices). Graphite is partly specular, so under a point source the darkest region of the page becomes the brightest. This defeats our normalisation in a specific way: a highlight on one bubble raises its brightness and lowers its fill ratio while leaving max(fill) untouched, so a genuinely shaded bubble falls under 0.65 and scores blank. Defence in three parts. Detect: count pixels at or above 250 of 255 inside each bubble disc, and when more than about 5% of the disc is blown, that bubble has no measurable fill ratio, so the question is uncertain and is shown to the teacher, never scored. Instruct: the viewfinder hint is ZipGrade's own remedy, move to the other side of the desk, because the physical fix is a step sideways and no exposure setting recovers information a mirror reflection destroyed. Prevent: print pen guidance on the sheet, recommending a black or blue gel or ballpoint pen or a soft 2B pencil and discouraging hard H and 2H pencils, since ink absorbs stably where graphite reflects unpredictably under LED light (https://electronics.alibaba.com/question/omr-machine-guide-how-it-works-what-to-consider).
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, plus one printed line on the sheet and one viewfinder hint in the interface
requirements.testable: Composite synthetic specular blobs of varying size and intensity over known-filled bubbles in golden images, and assert the engine flags uncertain rather than returning blank, at every blob size above the gate. Then shoot a real batch under a bare ceiling LED at three phone angles and count how many questions the glare detector flags versus how many it silently misreads with the detector disabled.

requirements.complaint: My own shadow fell across the paper and one question read wrongly, even though the rest of the sheet was fine.
requirements.defence: This is the boundary of rule 1, and it needs stating rather than discovering. A soft gradient across the page is exactly what intra-question normalisation was designed for and it handles that well; what it cannot handle is a hard shadow EDGE crossing a single question row, so that choice A sits in light and choice D sits in shade. Within that one row the paper-to-mark contrast differs between choices, and fill_i / max(fill) no longer means what it means elsewhere. The geometry makes this near-universal rather than exotic: the teacher must hold the phone between the ceiling light and the paper in order to frame it. Defence: we already have to locate the gaps between bubbles to sample discs, so measure paper-white luminance in the gutters at both ends of every question row. Normalise out the slow component per row, and when the two ends of one row differ by more than a calibrated fraction, that question is uncertain rather than answered. Also add the physical hint ZipGrade and CamScanner both give, which is to raise the phone, because a more distant camera casts a smaller and softer shadow.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, per question row
requirements.testable: Generate synthetic half-shadow images sweeping the step magnitude from 5% to 60% of paper white, find the magnitude at which any answer flips, and set the gate below it with margin. Then verify on real photos taken deliberately with the teacher's body between an overhead lamp and the desk: every question the gate flags should be one a human agrees is unreadable in that frame.

requirements.complaint: The picture always looks dull and grey and the light pencil marks vanish into it, and indoors there are faint stripes across the frame.
requirements.defence: Two camera-configuration facts, neither of which any OMR vendor I found talks about. First, reflected-light meters render what they see as about 18% grey, so an answer sheet filling the viewfinder is a near-white field that auto exposure pulls down to mid grey, the same way a camera turns snow grey and needs roughly +1 EV (https://www.cambridgeincolour.com/tutorials/camera-metering.htm). Because our threshold is relative, the SCORE often survives; what does not survive is the width of the grey band, because compressed contrast pushes more bubbles into the uncertain zone and turns a scan into a review queue. Defence: drive exposure from the sheet's own reference patches rather than the scene average. The four 8 mm solid black fiducials give a black point and the surrounding paper gives a white point, both in frame and both of known reflectance, so lock AE to put paper white at roughly 200 to 220 of 255. Second, all AC lighting modulates at twice mains, which is 100 Hz on the 50 Hz grid used in Saudi Arabia, so a rolling-shutter readout that is not an integer multiple of that cycle produces horizontal brightness bands that fall across question rows and change the relative brightness of bubbles within one question. Enable platform anti-banding at 50 Hz and pin exposure to a multiple of 10 ms. Then keep a residual detector: measure paper white row by row in the gutters, and if periodic ripple exceeds about 3%, the frame is not measurable. Note the bad interaction with rule 3 in both directions: band phase drifts between frames, so either three frames never agree and the scan appears to hang, or three frames band alike and agree on a wrong reading.
requirements.where: interface, in the camera configuration, not in core-omr
requirements.testable: In a fluorescent-lit room, assert the paper-white histogram peak lands between 190 and 230 and row-to-row luminance ripple stays under 3% across 100 consecutive frames. Compare the count of bubbles landing in the grey band under locked versus default exposure on the same papers; the locked configuration should measurably shrink the review queue, and that delta is the number that justifies the work.

requirements.complaint: The app sits there saying it is waiting for focus, and the closer I hold the phone the blurrier it gets.
requirements.defence: This is device-class specific and total where it applies. The react-native-vision-camera issue tracker reports that on iPhone 15 Pro an app 'can't automatically switch to the macro lens (the ultra wide lens), so it can't focus small documents', that the same failure shows in other third-party scanning apps, and that Apple's position is that the app is at fault for using only the main camera, which on 14 and 15 Pro cannot focus close (https://github.com/mrousavy/react-native-vision-camera/issues/2246). Adobe Scan users report the same (https://community.adobe.com/t5/adobe-scan-discussions/iphone-15-pro-max-won-t-focus-on-small-documents/m-p/14218668). This is directly load-bearing because our stack is vision-camera v5. Defence: at session start, read the device's minimumFocusDistance, pick the lens and derive the zoom factor from it rather than assuming the main camera, and compute the required working distance from the code module rather than from the bubbles (see the resolution requirement). Gate on a sharpness statistic measured on the fiducial edges, which are known high-contrast step edges of known size, rather than on a global blur score over a page that is mostly white paper. When the gate fails, name the condition instead of exposing a threshold slider.
requirements.where: interface, in the camera configuration
requirements.testable: A device matrix covering at least one multi-camera iPhone Pro, one older single-camera iPhone, one flagship Android and one budget Android: assert focus lock within 2 seconds at the computed working distance for A4 and for A6, and assert the fiducial-edge sharpness statistic separates a hand-blurred frame from a sharp one with no overlap across 200 frames per device.

requirements.complaint: It reads the bubbles fine but says it cannot identify the sheet, and I have no idea what that means.
requirements.defence: The resolution floor is set by the printed code, not by the bubbles, and this is counter-intuitive enough to belong in the spec comments. codeModuleMm is 0.5 and radiusMm is 2, so at the standard warp of 4.76 px/mm a bubble is 19 px across, which is ample, while a code module is 2.38 px, which is at or below the three to four pixels per module that decoders need before error correction starts working hard. Worse, the pipeline as written resizes by 0.25 before anything else: on a 1080p frame with the sheet filling it, the source is about 0.84 px/mm, so a bubble is 3.4 px and a module is 0.42 px, and warping that up to 1000x1414 restores nothing. The fix is a rule: the quarter-scale frame exists to FIND the sheet, and nothing else. Scale the homography back by 4 and take the code decode, the fill ratios and the timing marks from the full-resolution frame. Then the sensor requirement follows: three pixels per module needs 6 px/mm on the page, which is 1260 px across A4's short side, so 1080p gives 5.14 px/mm and 2.6 px per module and is marginal, 1440p gives 3.4 and works, 4K gives 5.1 and is comfortable. Select a frame format of at least 1440p and accept the frame-rate cost. On the scanner path the same arithmetic gives 3.9 px per module at 200 dpi and 5.9 at 300, so document 200 dpi as the minimum and 300 dpi whenever code is 'full'. Vendors disagree about OMR resolution precisely because of this split: Addmen says 100 dpi is enough for bubbles but 150 to 200 once a sheet carries a machine-readable code (https://www.addmengroup.com/omr-scanner/how-to-scan-omr-sheets.htm), and Remark says 200 to 300 for the same reason (https://remarksoftware.com/support/remark-office-omr-support/scanner-information/). Finally, when the code fails to decode but four fiducials are found, measure px/mm from the fiducial spacing and say 'too far away to read the sheet code' rather than 'sheet not recognised'.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, plus one camera format decision in the interface
requirements.testable: A pure unit test that renders the code for a full payload, downsamples it to simulate 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 dpi and the 4.76 px/mm warp, and asserts the decode rate at each, gated in CI so nobody quietly lowers the warp resolution later. Then on device, log px/mm at lock across the device matrix and assert the tenth percentile stays above 6 px/mm.

requirements.complaint: I scanned the same paper twice and got two different scores, exactly like the competitor did.
requirements.defence: Our rule already says every bubble returns a ratio and the grey band flags uncertainty. What is missing is the number: 0.65 and 0.45 are asserted, not measured, and there is no stated hysteresis. Finding 49 is precisely a near-threshold bubble, an eraser scar or a stray pen touch, read one way at 21:59 and another at 22:01, and the competitive notes are right that this is the commonest case in real papers rather than a rare fault. Defence: derive the band from data instead of asserting it. On the golden set, hand-label bubbles as filled, blank, erased, or stray mark, and measure the ratio distribution of each class. Separately, using the repeat shots that criterion 8 already requires, measure the shot-to-shot standard deviation of the same physical bubble's ratio. Set the band edges so the band is at least four times that standard deviation wide, and verify that no bubble's ratio crosses a band edge between two shots of the same paper. Publish both numbers in the accuracy methodology, since section 8b commits us to publishing our real measurements as a GEO advantage; a measured band width is a far stronger claim than a threshold pair.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, with the numbers produced by the golden set process
requirements.testable: A CI report, not just a pass or fail, printing the measured shot-to-shot sigma and the band width in sigmas, failing the build if the ratio drops below 4. Add a dedicated golden-set subset of erased and lightly-shaded bubbles, hand-labelled, with at least three shots each, and assert that every one is either the same decision in all three shots or flagged uncertain in all three.

requirements.complaint: I printed one master and photocopied the rest for the whole class, and now some read badly.
requirements.defence: Change one printed string and rely on an existing check. The sheet currently warns to print at 100% and not to use fit to page. It does not warn against photocopying, and those are different failures: scaling is uniform and recoverable, while a copier re-images through its own optics and paper path, changing scale, registration and tone, and compounding with each generation. Institutional guidance is explicit that staff should print multiple copies of the template rather than photocopy a printed sheet (https://teach.its.uiowa.edu/gradescope/gradescope-bubble-sheets). Photocopying a master is the natural teacher behaviour, so the warning has to name it. Detection is already paid for by the scale and anisotropy check, since a copy shows up as anisotropic scale or drifting row pitch; the printed line simply moves the cheapest fix upstream of the failure. Cost is a string in the 12 mm warning band, in Arabic and English, so it belongs in the same version bump as the geometry changes.
requirements.where: sheet design (the printed warning band), detected by the scale check in the pipeline
requirements.testable: Photocopy a printed sheet on a real office multifunction, first and second generation, from two different machines, and put all four in the golden set. Assert every one is either graded correctly or refused with the scale or stretch reason, and that none is graded wrongly. In beta, ask the 20 teachers directly whether they photocopied; the answer sizes the risk better than any published source I could find.

requirements.complaint: The app said the scan was good and it agreed with itself three times, and it was still wrong.
requirements.defence: Two changes to what agreement means, one to the pipeline and one to the acceptance criteria. In the pipeline, reorder: each frame must independently pass the physical gates, which are focus, glare, banding, scale, timing residual and mark census, and only then does three-frames-agree act as a tie-breaker on the answer string. Agreement between three frames of one bad pose is not evidence; a steady slow sweep produces three similarly-skewed frames that agree with each other, and a flicker band can hold phase for three frames. In the acceptance criteria, give criterion 8 a twin. Criterion 8 requires three shots of every golden paper to give the same result, which is right and should stay. Criterion 8b requires a deliberately adversarial subset where all three shots agree and the correct behaviour is refusal: a paper with a synthetic dust line, a paper with a fixed specular highlight in all three shots, a paper photocopied at 94% in all three shots. If the build can grade any of those, then the team has learned that agreement is the guarantee, which is the wrong lesson, and the criterion exists to prevent that lesson being learned.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline ordering, and process (section 11 acceptance criteria)
requirements.testable: The criterion is its own test. Ten adversarial golden papers, three shots each, all consistent, all required to refuse. Plus a unit test asserting that the frame-acceptance function rejects a frame failing any physical gate before any agreement logic is consulted, so the ordering cannot be quietly inverted in a later refactor.

requirements.complaint: Every scan is now a refusal or a review, and it was faster to grade them by hand.
requirements.defence: Every requirement above converts a silent error into a refusal or an uncertain flag, and that ratchet only turns one way. A scanner that refuses 30% of papers is worse to use than one that guesses, and nothing in the current acceptance criteria notices that happening, because 99.7% accuracy and zero silent errors are both satisfied by a product that refuses almost everything. Defence: measure the cost of caution as a first-class number. On the ordinary-conditions subset of the golden set, cap refusals at 2% of papers and uncertain flags at 1% of questions, and report both alongside accuracy on every CI run. On the adversarial subset, invert the requirement: refusal is the pass. Publish the ordinary-conditions numbers with the accuracy claim, since a refusal rate is exactly the kind of documented statistic section 8b commits us to.
requirements.where: process (CI gates and the published methodology)
requirements.testable: Two counters in the same CI report as the accuracy figure, with the golden set explicitly partitioned into ordinary and adversarial subsets so the two ceilings cannot be gamed by moving images between them. In closed beta, log papers scanned per minute per teacher; if the median drops below roughly one paper every five seconds, a gate is too tight regardless of what the golden set says.

requirements.complaint: Our copier scans everything in black and white, or the photo came from WhatsApp, and the results are strange.
requirements.defence: This is the sharpest architectural collision in the whole survey. Other vendors accept bitonal input because their engines make a boolean decision per bubble; Remark actively prefers black and white over greyscale (https://remarksoftware.com/support/remark-office-omr-support/scanner-information/). Ours cannot. Our entire design rests on every bubble returning a ratio and on a grey band that flags uncertainty, and a bitonal scan has already been thresholded upstream by a device-specific algorithm at a single cut before we see it. In a two-level image the grey band cannot exist: every bubble is 0.0 or 1.0 and the uncertainty machinery silently reports total confidence, which is the worst possible failure mode for a product whose promise is that it never guesses. Copier defaults push the same way: Canon documents that auto exposure 'may not produce clear copies on light or faint originals (e.g. pencil written work)' (https://support.usa.canon.com/kb/s/article/ART126394), and Xerox background suppression is designed to remove exactly the variation we measure. Defence: a bitonal image is trivially identifiable from its histogram, so refuse it on admission, or accept it in an explicitly degraded mode that is labelled in the UI and excluded from every published accuracy claim. The same admission gate covers recompressed imports, where JPEG ringing puts overshoot rings around every printed bubble outline and biases a mean-of-dark-pixels fill ratio, most for empty bubbles whose only dark content is the outline (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/238440938_Removal_of_artifacts_from_JPEG_compressed_document_images). Publish greyscale or colour at 300 dpi as a hard requirement of the PDF path, not a recommendation. Note the live camera path is already safe by design because the frame processor reads YUV, and that should be written down as a rule rather than left as an implementation detail.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline admission check, gating the post-MVP PDF and gallery import path
requirements.testable: Convert the whole golden set to 1-bit and assert every image is refused rather than graded. Then re-encode the golden set at JPEG quality 90, 70, 50 and 30 and measure the actual fill-ratio shift per bubble class; that measurement decides the quality floor, because I found the mechanism documented for text but no published magnitude for a printed bubble outline.

requirements.complaint: The copier changed what was on the page.
requirements.defence: This is the strongest refusal case in the survey and it is not hypothetical. A computer scientist found Xerox WorkCentres substituting digits in scanned building plans (https://www.dkriesel.com/en/blog/2013/0802_xerox-workcentres_are_switching_written_numbers_when_scanning), and Xerox first said the bug occurred only at the lowest quality setting, then 'determined that the factory default and highest modes do not completely alleviate the problem of substituting characters' (https://www.computerworld.com/article/1504935/the-xerox-character-substitution-bug-is-worse-than-first-thought.html), while shipping MRC compression enabled by default (https://www.support.xerox.com/en-us/article/en/2108786). JBIG2 and MRC build a dictionary of image patches judged similar and reuse one representative in place of the others. An answer sheet is the worst conceivable input for that: hundreds of near-identical small circles differing only in how full they are, so the compressor is licensed to substitute a filled bubble for an empty one, and the result is internally consistent and looks perfectly correct. Defence: a PDF whose images are JBIG2-coded or MRC-layered is not evidence of what a student marked. Inspect the image XObject filters and refuse the file before decoding a single page, telling the teacher to rescan with compression turned down. This alone means the PDF path is a distinct intake with its own admission rules, not a thin decoder bolted in front of the same engine.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline, at the PDF container level, before any image decoding
requirements.testable: A fixture set of PDFs produced by real multifunction devices at factory defaults, at least one Xerox with MRC on and one with JBIG2, asserted refused by filter inspection. Plus a synthetic proof for the team: take a clean sheet image, run it through a JBIG2 encoder at an aggressive setting, and show the substituted bubbles side by side, because this is the finding people will not believe until they see it.

requirements.complaint: Every paper in the class has a thin line down it and a few of them scored oddly.
requirements.defence: HP states that '99% of all lines and streaks on copies made by feeding the original documents through the ADF are caused by debris on the ADF glass' (https://support.hp.com/us-en/document/c06432233), listing dust, toner, adhesive residue, correction fluid and fingerprints. The ADF images a moving page through a narrow fixed glass strip, so one speck prints a line down the entire length of every page in the batch at the same x on all of them. Three consequences: a line at the wrong x runs through a bubble column and adds constant dark bias to one choice on every question of every paper; a line near the left edge can be mistaken for timing marks; and, most importantly, it is identical on every page and reproduces perfectly on a rescan, so it passes criterion 8 and would pass three-frames-agree. This is the clearest available proof that determinism is necessary and not sufficient, and it is the case I would use to teach the team that lesson. Defence is cheap: after warping, look for a full-height dark column one to four pixels wide at near-constant x, and confirm it by checking that the same x recurs across at least three pages of the batch. Refuse the batch with 'clean the scanner glass', which is a fix the teacher performs in ten seconds. Alongside it, publish recommended driver settings for the PDF path, since the scanner's own helpfulness is the enemy here: auto-crop off, deskew off, auto-rotate off, blank-page removal off, compression off, greyscale, 300 dpi. Note that plain feeder skew itself is not our enemy, since four fiducials plus a homography handle rotation exactly; what hurts is what the driver does about skew on our behalf, and our four solid black squares sitting near the paper edge are exactly the dark-near-the-margin feature that triggers aggressive auto-crop.
requirements.where: scanner pipeline (per page and per batch), with a documented settings page in process
requirements.testable: Composite a 2 px black column at a bubble-column x onto every image of a golden batch and assert the batch is refused. Then assert the counterfactual: grading the same batch with the detector disabled changes at least one answer on at least one paper, and gives the identical wrong answer on a rescan, which is the demonstration that criterion 8 alone would have passed it.

requirements.complaint: I scanned thirty papers and only twenty-eight students have grades, and nobody can tell me which two are missing.
requirements.defence: No software in the image can fix this, because the missing page produced no pixels. Three mechanisms delete a student silently: a double feed sends two sheets through as one so the inner sheet is never imaged; blank-page removal discards pages the driver judges empty, with vendors warning explicitly that 'almost blank documents with only a few characters' may be detected as blank (https://www.pfu.ricoh.com/imaging/downloads/manual/ss_webhelp/en/help/webhelp/topic/tb_img_all_blank.html), which describes exactly the paper of a student who answered three questions; and duplex-by-default turns every single-sided sheet into a real page plus a blank one. The safeguards are routinely switched off, since HP instructs users that if the scanner falsely detects a multi-pick 'it will be necessary to turn off the detection feature' (https://support.hp.com/us-en/document/c03257453). Defence is counting, not vision. Rule 8 already establishes reconcile-before-create for duplicates; absence is its mirror and is currently unwritten. The PDF path reports pages in versus sheets read versus sheets refused, and where a class roster exists it names the students with no paper: 'thirty pages, twenty-eight sheets read, two unaccounted for' beats a silent success. This also strengthens the camera path, where the same reconciliation against the roster catches the paper a teacher simply forgot to photograph.
requirements.where: interface (batch reconciliation view) and process, riding with the PDF import path
requirements.testable: Feed a PDF with one page removed, one page duplicated, and one page replaced by a blank, and assert the reconciliation banner reports each case distinctly and names the missing student where the roster allows. Assert that a batch with any unaccounted page cannot be marked complete without an explicit acknowledgement from the teacher.

requirements.complaint: I was sweeping the phone across a stack and it locked while I was still moving.
requirements.defence: Every smartphone uses a rolling shutter, reading rows sequentially across roughly a 15 to 35 ms window (https://www.cizucu.com/en/magazines/2026-02-learn-how-to-fix-flicker-banding), so a phone that translates or rotates during readout photographs the top and bottom of the page from different viewpoints. The frame is then not a single planar perspective projection, and getPerspectiveTransform is fitting a model the data does not obey, yet all four fiducials are found cleanly and the warp is wrong in the middle of the page where the bubbles are. Order of magnitude: at 10 degrees per second of pan, a 15 to 35 ms readout gives 0.15 to 0.35 degrees of skew, which at a 190 mm half-width is around a millimetre of displacement at the far edge, comparable to a bubble radius. The timing-residual gate already catches this as a monotonic residual down the page, which is why this is a watch item rather than a requirement: it is a cheaper preventive using expo-sensors to drop frames captured while angular rate exceeds a few degrees per second, and it is worth adding only if beta shows the residual gate rejecting an annoying number of otherwise-good frames. Reasoning rather than citation on the OMR consequence; the rolling-shutter mechanism itself is well documented.
requirements.where: interface, in the camera pipeline before the homography
requirements.testable: Instrument beta builds to log gyroscope angular rate at the moment of every frame that the residual gate rejects. If rejected frames cluster at high angular rate, a motion gate converts those rejections into a smoother experience; if they do not, the gate would only slow the loop down and should not be built.

requirements.complaint: The sheet code needs a good camera and a 300 dpi scan, and some of our users have neither.
requirements.defence: codeModuleMm is 0.5, which is the constant that sets the working distance for the phone and the dpi floor for the scanner, both tighter than the bubbles require. The alternative is to spend paper instead of pixels: raising the module to 0.7 mm gives 3.3 px per module at the standard warp with no pipeline heroics at all. The catch is codeMaxSizeMm 30 and the quiet zone of 4 modules each side. A version 3 code, 29 modules plus 8 of quiet zone, is 18.5 mm at 0.5 and 25.9 mm at 0.7, both fitting. A larger version needed by a rich 'full' payload, say 41 modules plus quiet zone, is 24.5 mm at 0.5 and 34 mm at 0.7, which breaks the 30 mm cap and would force the sheet to be refused as too complex to describe itself. So the module size and the payload size are one decision, not two, and the honest move is to fix the pipeline first, measure real decode rates on real devices in beta, and only then decide whether to spend a millimetre of paper or trim the payload. Reasoning, not citation, on the payload arithmetic; the three-to-four pixels per module decode floor is the well-attested part.
requirements.where: sheet design (GEOMETRY.codeModuleMm) traded against the payload the code carries
requirements.testable: Before touching the constant, log decode success rate and px/mm at lock across the beta device fleet for a month. Raise the module only if the tenth-percentile device fails to decode more than a small fraction of the time after the full-resolution ROI fix. Any change here is a printed-artifact change and bumps the spec version, so it should be batched with any other sheet change rather than shipped alone.

defences.alreadyCovered:
Seven complaints in this research are genuinely answered by decisions already in the plan, and repeating them would be self-congratulation.

Slow illumination gradients and general shadow across a page. Rule 1, the relative-within-question threshold, handles this correctly and is the right call. The research does not weaken it; it only fences it, at the hard shadow EDGE inside a single row, which is a different physical thing and gets its own requirement above.

Plain skew and rotation, from a handheld angle or a worn ADF roller. Four solid fiducials plus getPerspectiveTransform handle rotation exactly. Brother's ADF Auto Deskew tops out at 5 degrees (https://help.brother-usa.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/149584), but that is a driver limit and irrelevant to us: we would rather the driver left the skew alone. Nothing to build. What does need attention is not the skew but what the driver does about it, and that sits inside the dust-line and settings requirement.

Two shaded bubbles on a select:'one' question. Rule 2 already stops and shows the teacher, and the deliberate select:'many' exception already keeps a check-all-that-apply question from being called ambiguous. Competitor finding 49 involves a double mark, but the half of it that hurt was not detection of the double mark, it was whether the second mark is seen consistently between two scans, which the grey-band calibration requirement addresses.

A blank student id read as zero. Rule 9 already makes this an explicit unset state with a warning. This was the competitor's ID: 0 and we recorded it correctly.

A rescan creating a second contradictory record. Rule 8, reconcile before create, plus acceptance criterion 9, already cover this. Batch reconciliation for MISSING papers is the untouched mirror of it, which is why that requirement is framed as extending an existing principle rather than inventing one.

Recompression damage on the live camera path. Because the frame processor reads YUV frames directly, the JPEG block and ringing artefacts that hurt imported images never reach the live engine. That is currently an implementation detail and it should be written down as a rule so a later refactor to a still-capture API does not quietly discard it.

The teacher not knowing why a sheet will not lock. Scan-loop item 1, the four corners lighting up as they are found, already answers this for the case where the corners are not found, and it was one of the better things we took from the competitor. It answers nothing for the far more dangerous class of failures where all four corners ARE found and the reading is still untrustworthy, and that class is where most of this list lives.

Also worth recording: the frame-buffer and dispose rules 4 and 5 already prevent the camera stalling under load, and nothing in this research touches them. And the image-minimisation decision, no upload and no storage, incidentally removes an entire family of failures around server-side recompression that other products have to live with.
defences.cannotDefend:
Seven things no amount of software fixes. In each case the answer is the same shape, and it is worth saying plainly that this shape is a feature: refusing clearly, naming the physical condition, and telling the teacher the ten-second fix beats a plausible number every time. A product that says 'clean the scanner glass' is more trustworthy than one that says nothing and is quietly wrong on every paper in the batch.

A page that was fed but never imaged. A double feed produces no pixels, so no image analysis can recover it. We count instead: pages in versus sheets read, reconciled against the roster, with the missing students named.

A page the driver deleted before we opened the file. Blank-page removal discards the paper of a student who answered three questions, and the vendor documentation says so. Again only counting catches it, and the counting has to live at the batch level because a single image cannot know it has siblings.

A copier that substituted patches under JBIG2 or MRC. The output is internally consistent and looks correct; there is nothing in the pixels that reveals a filled bubble was swapped for an empty one. We refuse the container by its compression filter, before decoding, and never grade it.

A bitonal scan. The grey information was destroyed upstream by a device-specific threshold and cannot be recovered by any amount of processing. Our uncertainty machinery would report total confidence on an image that contains none. We refuse, or we grade in a mode explicitly labelled degraded and excluded from every published accuracy claim.

Glare. A specular reflection of a lamp is not a processing artefact, it is missing information: the region is saturated and there is no measurement to recover. We detect the saturation, refuse the question, and tell the teacher to move to the other side of the desk, which is the fix ZipGrade also gives because it is the only one that exists. Upstream we do the one preventive thing available, which is printing pen guidance on the sheet, since ink absorbs where graphite reflects.

Print scaling applied by a driver without telling the application. Adobe documents this in its own words, so our printed warning is advice that cannot be enforced at the point where it matters. We measure the printed result instead and refuse with the measured percentage, which is also the only way a teacher ever learns which of the twenty controls in the print dialog was wrong.

A genuinely ambiguous physical page: a hard pencil pressed lightly, an incomplete erasure, a stray pen touch. There is no ground truth in the image, so any confident answer would be an invention. This is precisely what the grey band is for, and the honest position is that our job is to hand the teacher the paper and the crop and let a human decide, never to resolve it silently in either direction. Widening our defences here does not mean guessing better, it means measuring how wide the ambiguous zone really is, which is why the grey-band calibration requirement asks for a number rather than a rule.

One more that is worth naming even though it is not a capture condition: we have no field data on how often any of this happens in Saudi classrooms. Every user voice in this research is English-language and mostly North American or South Asian; an Arabic-language search for teachers describing these failures returned nothing usable. The 20-teacher closed beta in weeks 13 and 14 is therefore not a polish exercise, it is the only measurement of prevalence we will ever have before launch, and it should be instrumented to log which refusal reasons fire, how often, and whether the teacher succeeds on the next attempt.

defences.angle:
Printing, turned into engineering decisions for TransferChecker. I read PLAN.md §4 and §11, COMPETITIVE-NOTES §5, paper.ts, spec.ts, layout/index.ts, layout/grid.ts and core-omr/src/index.ts (still an empty stub — which is the single most important scheduling fact here: every rule below is free to change today and version-locked forever after the first sheet is printed in the wild).

Two things reframed the whole angle once I put the research numbers against our actual constants.

FIRST, the geometry is arithmetically wrong at the bottom edge, not arguably wrong. GEOMETRY.marginMm 6 + fiducialMm 8 puts each corner square between 6 mm and 14 mm from the paper edge. The general desktop unprintable limit is quoted at 6.35 mm (1/4 inch), so on an ordinary laser the outer 0.35 mm of all four squares is already clipped; entry-level inkjets quote bottom margins of 15 mm (Epson cut-sheet default) to 16.7 mm (Canon PIXMA MG2560), which swallows the band from H-16.7 to H entirely — and our bottom fiducials live at H-14 to H-6, wholly inside it. Both bottom corner squares simply do not exist on those printers. Worse, layout/index.ts puts warningAnchor at H - marginMm - fiducialMm - 3 = H-17 mm, roughly 0.3 mm above that same dead zone. So on the printer that kills us, the print warning is the LAST thing that survives: the teacher holds a sheet that looks complete, carries its "print at 100%" instruction intact, and has no bottom corners. That is not a warning problem, it is a layout problem, and it fails identically on all 120 copies.

SECOND, non-negotiable rule 1 ("relative within the question, never absolute") has two blind spots that print quality walks straight into, and I checked them against the exact rule in §4 (answer if >0.65 with no second >0.45, over fill_i/max(fill)). (a) A genuinely blank question has no answer, but max(fill) is always 1.0 by construction, so a blank row either reports as ambiguous — flooding review on every skipped question — or, when one bubble is meaningfully darker than its neighbours because of show-through, an eraser ghost or a stray pen dot, that noise normalises to 1.0 and the rest to ~0.3 and it is DECLARED AN ANSWER. That is a silent wrong answer, the exact class of defect we condemn in finding 43. (b) §4 itself says we display "عدد الفراغات", the count of blanks, but the rule as written has no way to produce a blank state at all. The fix keeps the spirit of rule 1 completely: the references stay on the page (fiducial ink for black, page whitespace and the median bubble for white), so the floor is absolute in ink terms and still fully relative in luminance terms, which is what actually defeats shadow. This one change also absorbs show-through, dot gain, toner-save and coloured stock at once, which is why it leads the list rather than any print-side patch.

Everything else follows from one distinction the research made available and no competitor exploits: a uniform print scale is HARMLESS to us (the homography eats it, as it eats the forensically documented 1-2% photocopy distortion), while a clipped mark, a faint mark and a curled sheet are fatal. The entire industry bans scaling, which is the one thing that does not matter, and says nothing measurable about the three that do. Sources for every printer number are the ones supplied in the findings; my own additions are marked as reasoning. My web-search budget was exhausted before I could add citations of my own, so no claim below rests on a URL I have not been handed.

requirements.complaint: A blank question, a show-through disc from the back of the sheet, or an eraser ghost gets read as the student's answer — or every skipped question floods the teacher with 'review this'.
requirements.defence: Add an absolute ink floor underneath the relative rule, with both references taken from the page itself so shadow immunity is untouched. black_ref = mean ink of the four 8 mm fiducials (the only guaranteed-solid black on the sheet); empty_ref = median fill across every bubble on the page (on a select:'one' sheet with 4-5 choices, 75-80% of bubbles are empty, so the median is solidly an empty bubble). A question is BLANK, a first-class state, when (max_fill - empty_ref) / (black_ref - empty_ref) < floor; start the floor at 0.25 and tune it on the golden set. Only above the floor does fill_i/max(fill) and the 0.65 / 0.45 pair run. This gives three outcomes where §4 has two: answered, blank, ambiguous — and it is what makes §4's own promised 'عدد الفراغات' counter computable at all.
requirements.where: scanning pipeline (core-omr, still an empty stub, so this costs nothing today)
requirements.testable: Golden-set cases with known-blank rows: assert state 'blank', never an answer and never 'ambiguous'. A duplex-on-20lb subset where the reverse side is fully shaded behind a blank row: assert blank. Property test: for any bubble vector whose spread is below the floor, the result is blank regardless of which bubble is darkest — i.e. no permutation of near-equal noise can produce an answer.

requirements.complaint: The bubbles print fatter than on screen and my papers throw far more 'uncertain' flags than my colleague's.
requirements.defence: Subtract the empty baseline before normalising: (fill_i - empty_ref) / (max_fill - empty_ref) instead of fill_i / max(fill). Inkjet dot gain and feathering thicken the printed 2 mm-radius bubble outline, which raises the empty-bubble dark ratio uniformly; the current ratio only partly cancels that and the residue compresses the gap between filled and empty, squeezing more bubbles into the 0.45-0.65 grey band. Baseline subtraction turns a uniformly raised floor into a cancelled constant and restores the decision margin. Same code path as the floor above, so implement them together, once.
requirements.where: scanning pipeline
requirements.testable: Print one identical spec on a laser and on an inkjet on cheap absorbent copier paper, shade identically, measure the empty-bubble fill ratio on both, and assert the count of uncertain-band bubbles differs by no more than a small fixed number across the two — not merely that the scores match.

requirements.complaint: The bottom two black squares are missing from my printout and I did nothing wrong.
requirements.defence: Stop using one symmetric margin. The homography needs four points at KNOWN positions, not four points at EQUAL insets, and the scanner reads those positions from the printed code, so asymmetry is geometrically free — it costs page area only. Proposal: top and sides 10 mm (clears the 6.35 mm general desktop limit with 3.65 mm of placement slack, and the 4.23 mm HP LaserJet figure with room to spare), bottom 18 mm (clears Canon's 16.7 mm and Epson's 15 mm). Cost on A4 is about 12 mm of grid height, roughly one row at pitchYMm 7. Ship it as the default rather than an option, because the teacher who needs it is exactly the teacher who will not know to tick a box. Also move warningAnchor up with it; today it sits at H-17 mm, about 0.3 mm above the dead zone, so on the printer that kills us the warning is the last thing standing.
requirements.where: sheet design (GEOMETRY in paper.ts — a printed-artifact constant, so this is a SheetSpec.version bump after launch and free before it)
requirements.testable: Print the same PDF on three or four cheap printers spanning laser and entry-level inkjet, then measure the printed inset of every corner square with a ruler and assert all four are complete on all machines. Cheaper first pass with no hardware: render at the quoted margins and assert no fiducial pixel falls inside a 16.7 mm bottom / 6.35 mm elsewhere exclusion rectangle.

requirements.complaint: Row 34 got read as row 33 on some of the papers.
requirements.defence: Raise GEOMETRY.timingHeightMm from 3 to 4 and move the track inboard with the new margin (it currently starts at x = marginMm = 6, sharing the corner squares' clipping exposure). The adjacent-domain guidance supplied gives an OMR bar height of 4 mm to 12 mm with taller bars buying skew tolerance, so 3 mm is below the floor every cited source states. A 3 mm mark is also the first feature to break into a blob under EconoMode or on a third-generation copy, and a merged or lost timing mark is an off-by-one on row identity — a silent wrong answer for the whole column, not a visible failure. Version-locked constant, so decide it now.
requirements.where: sheet design (paper.ts) plus a row-index consistency check in the pipeline
requirements.testable: Golden-set cases at deliberately faint print and copy generation 3 that assert ROW INDEXING, not only the score: shade a single known row per sheet and assert the answered row index, so an off-by-one cannot hide behind a coincidentally equal total. Add an invariant that the count of detected timing marks equals rowsPerColumn, and refuse the scan when it does not.

requirements.complaint: The little square barcode does not read on the copies, or after the school turned on toner save.
requirements.defence: Two changes, both free. (1) Grow the module to fill the budget instead of pinning it at the floor. layout/index.ts currently computes codeSizeMm = (moduleCount + 8) * 0.5 with codeModuleMm fixed at its documented MINIMUM of 0.5 mm, against a codeMaxSizeMm of 30 mm. A typical full-geometry payload lands well under that ceiling, so a sheet with spare budget prints a needlessly fragile code; scale the module up to the largest value that keeps the code inside 30 mm. A 0.66 mm module is a third more ink per feature for zero page cost. (2) Use the highest error-correction level the payload allows, since we choose code size from payload anyway. The published quiet-zone rule (4 modules = 2.0 mm at 0.5 mm) is already met exactly, so the static design is right and the exposure is purely dynamic degradation. This matters more for us than for anyone else: 'full' mode is what makes the sheet gradeable by a device that has never seen the template, so our offline-first promise rides on the smallest printed feature on the page.
requirements.where: sheet design (layout/index.ts sizing, GEOMETRY.codeModuleMm semantics)
requirements.testable: A dedicated golden-set axis: decode rate versus copy generation (original, gen 1, gen 2, gen 3) crossed with normal print and EconoMode. Assert 100% decode through gen 2 at both module sizes and report the gen-3 delta, which is the number that justifies the change.

requirements.complaint: Nobody told me how to check the print before I ran off 120 copies.
requirements.defence: Print a 100 mm calibration bar with 10 mm ticks in the warning band, labelled in both scripts, with the instruction 'ضع مسطرة: يجب أن يقرأ 100 مم'. The research found this position completely unoccupied in OMR while it is routine in graph paper, sewing patterns, blueprints and printable rulers. It is the only element on the sheet that measures itself against an external standard: fit-to-page shrinks the bar along with everything else, and that is exactly what makes it work — the ruler reads 96 mm and the teacher reprints before making copies. The warning band is 12 mm tall, which fits a ~3 mm bar plus text. A credit-card outline (85.6 x 54 mm) does not fit and coin diameters for our market are unverified, so the ruler bar is the whole of the MVP version.
requirements.where: sheet design (warning band) and the teacher's process
requirements.testable: Render at 100%, 96% and 94% and measure the printed bar with a ruler on real paper; assert it reads 100, 96 and 94 mm. Then the human test that actually matters: hand five beta teachers an unlabelled sheet printed with fit-to-page on and ask them to tell you whether it is safe to copy.

requirements.complaint: I printed the sheet and the app just will not recognise it. It looks fine to me.
requirements.defence: Ship a one-page printer check as page 1 of every sheet download: the four corner squares at their real insets, the 100 mm bar, and one line of instruction — 'if all four squares printed complete and the bar measures 100 mm, this printer is safe for TransferChecker'. One page, ten seconds, before the class set. This is the artefact the whole industry is missing: every vendor found ships an unverifiable instruction ('print at 100%') and AMC's own users are told there is no way to detect print scaling, only a tolerance knob to widen until the symptom disappears. A test page converts a hope into a measurement the teacher makes with the ruler already in the room.
requirements.where: sheet design (generator output) and the teacher's process
requirements.testable: Print the test page on the same three or four printers used for the margin test and confirm it correctly flags each machine that clips a corner. Beta metric: proportion of teachers who print the check page before the class set, measured by asking them, and the correlation with their first-scan failure rate.

requirements.complaint: It just sits there hunting and never locks. I do not know what it wants.
requirements.defence: Two additions to a loop we have already designed well. (1) Name the missing corner, not just the found ones. Finding 42 gives us corner highlighting; the diagnostic value is in the negative — 'الركن السفلي الأيسر غير موجود: قد تكون طابعتك تقصّه. اطبع صفحة الفحص' distinguishes a printer fault from an aiming fault, which is the distinction the teacher cannot make and we can. (2) Give the three-consecutive-frames rule a deadline. Glare tracking across the fiducials, or a curled sheet, can make frames disagree indefinitely, so the strictness that protects determinism becomes a hang. After ~2 s without agreement, stop and state the most likely cause from what the pipeline already knows: corners found but code not decoding, corners found but frames disagreeing, fewer than four corners, low page contrast.
requirements.where: interface (scan overlay) plus a small state machine in the pipeline
requirements.testable: Scripted failure cases: cover one corner, shine a lamp at a corner, present a curled sheet, present a faint copy. Assert each produces its own named message within 2 s and never an indefinite hunt. Add these four as UI snapshot cases so a refactor cannot quietly reduce them to one generic error.

requirements.complaint: It worked for my colleague in the US and not for me. / I printed on the yellow paper for that class.
requirements.defence: Fix what the teacher sees before the print dialog, since the driver decides silently. Put the paper name in the warning band in large type ('A4 — اطبع بالحجم الأصلي 100%، لا Fit to page'), add 'وجه واحد' and 'ورق أبيض عادي', name the PDF file with its paper size so the tray choice is in front of them, and default PAPER_FAMILIES from device locale (Gulf → A, US → LETTER) instead of asking. Keep the warning as a norm-setter and stop treating it as a control: a printed instruction cannot detect its own violation, and if fit-to-page shrank the page the warning shrank with it and still reads as correct. On coloured paper our honest line is not the industry's blanket 'never' — a uniform tint largely cancels in the relative rule and in adaptiveThreshold — but 'coloured paper is where the CODE stops decoding first', which is a specific, testable claim rather than folklore.
requirements.where: sheet design (warning band, file naming) and the interface (paper defaulting)
requirements.testable: Golden-set stock axis: white, light yellow, light green, at one print quality.
